title: Can the Resrve Bank swim against the global rising tide of interest rates?
text:
Tell us about your experience.

I've been in a running debate with fellow ABC economics nerd David Taylor about what the Reserve Bank will do with interest rates on September 29: to hike or hold?

To this point, I've been firmly in the hold camp and DT has generally been in favour of a hike.

Our office argument is a microcosm of the same debate playing out in banks, trading rooms and probably at the RBA headquarters.

The traders have swung decisively to a rate hike, priced in at an 87 per cent probability according to LSEG data.

The economists are more divided. Of the big four banks, so far, only NAB has a September rate rise as its "base case", but the other three expecting the RBA to wait until November all acknowledge the September meeting is very much "live".

So, what are the main arguments for and against a September rate hike in Australia?

Loading...

The key arguments for a September rate hike

First to the case for a rate hike sooner rather than later.

Australian inflation, like the US, is above our central bank's target band, which is 2-3 per cent here.

While the annual headline Consumer Price Index (the Australian Bureau of Statistics' key inflation measure) fell from 3.8 to 3.5% in July, that was higher than economists were predicting.

The RBA's preferred trimmed mean number, that strips out the most volatile price moves, also remained stuck at 3.6 per cent.

Moreover, the detail showed that services price rises remained stubbornly above the RBA's target, telling economists that there are domestic price pressures rather than just imported inflation from higher fuel costs.

Those inflation numbers, released in August, already had some economists pencilling in a rate rise for September, or at least the risk of one.

Then there were stronger than expected economic growth numbers.

The Australian economy grew 2.1 per cent over the 12 months to June, once again a bit ahead of economist forecasts.

Historically, 2.1 per cent is a pretty mediocre annual growth rate for Australia, but the RBA now reckons the nation's economic speed limit is about 2 per cent, due to very weak productivity.

One of the factors driving growth over the past year has been a surge in business investment, mostly led by AI and related data centre construction.

Could interest rates top 7pc? The artificial intelligence boom could push the global economy into "good deflation" as economic growth surges, but that could result in interest rates exceeding 7 per cent, according to a major technology investor.

This building frenzy is happening at such speed and there's so much cash behind it that crazy money is being hurled at tradespeople and technicians to get these things erected in a hurry, which is then flowing through to broader construction inflation.

Finally, today's US rate rise, on top of a move from the European Central Bank last week and the virtual certainty of one from the Bank of Japan tomorrow, is heaping pressure on the RBA to follow.

The relative fall in the Australian dollar against the currencies of countries that are raising rates will push up import costs and add to inflation, while also making Australia's exports a bit more competitive, adding to growth.

Australia's economy is very different from the US

So, the market's right? I hear you ask. A September rate rise is a done deal?

Not quite.

Australia is in quite a different position from the US.

First, as all the RBA's senior officials have pointed out repeatedly, our central bank has already raised rates three times this year.

Unlike post-COVID, where Australia lagged the rest of the developed world on rate rises, this time we are leading the way.

US Fed hikes interest rates to curb inflation The US economy has been dealing with years of higher-than-target inflation, and prices have surged in the wake of Mr Trump's war on Iran, his signature tariff policies and the ongoing AI boom.

Secondly, as US President Donald Trump was keen to point out in his Truth Social post this morning, the American economy is genuinely booming.

Unemployment is falling (most recently to 4.1 per cent), investment is surging and consumer spending is strong.

While the latter two are also broadly true for Australia, our jobs market is the inverse of the US.

Over there, the unemployment rate started the year at 4.3 per cent and has fallen to 4.1 per cent.

Here, the seasonally adjusted jobless rate started the year at 4.1 per cent and has risen to 4.5 per cent.

Australia is in a rapid housing downturn

A third key difference is the prevalence of variable-rate mortgages here, which has meant that the three rate rises early this year, along with major tax changes, have sent the housing market into a rapid reverse from last year's boom.

Chief economists Paul Bloxham from HSBC and David Bassanese from Betashares both expect the RBA to hike rates in September, but both also acknowledge the effect that is likely to have on housing.

"Further rate rises will add to the downward pressure on house prices, which in turn risks more substantial slowing in consumer spending and housing construction," Bassanese warns.

Bloxham now expects a national 13 per cent peak-to-trough fall in house prices, and explains there are four ways this will slow Australia's economy.

Data centre demand is flowing through to broader construction inflation. (ABC News: John Gunn)

There's the wealth effect, with every 5 per cent fall in house prices expected to reduce consumer spending by 0.8 per cent over two years.

"Our 13 per cent assumed peak-to-trough decline would mean around 0.4 per cent less GDP in two quarters, and 1 per cent less GDP over time," Bloxham notes.

There's less economic activity generated from fewer property transfers and moves.

"During the 9 per cent housing price decline between 2017 and 2019, ownership transfer costs fell 27 per cent, taking 0.4ppts off annual GDP growth," he observes.

Falling stamp duty revenues will eat into state budgets, potentially forcing spending cuts.

Finally, falling prices tend to stop a lot of property development in its tracks, especially when rates and building costs are rising too.

That will free up some workers for the data centre boom and keep something of a lid on construction costs, although fewer new dwellings won't help rental inflation.

Is the risk of moving rates too early greater than the risk of waiting?

There are two other questions the RBA board members need to ask before raising rates in September.

The first is, how much do they trust that monthly inflation read from July.

"The question is just how much is due to post financial year price adjustments and how much is a sustained increase in underlying inflationary pressure," Westpac's economists asked at the time of its release.

"The monthly CPI does not provide enough information to confirm this in either direction."

Waiting until the November meeting gives the RBA the chance to get the full September quarter data, which it trusts far more than the relatively new monthly figures.

The second is how far the RBA can push rates before something in the economy snaps.

The RBA will have to decide how far it can push rates before something in the economy snaps. (ABC News: Kylie Silvester)

There was evidence that a lot of recent home buyers were struggling with their mortgage repayments the last time the cash rate was 4.35 per cent.

The cash rate hasn't been at 4.6 per cent or above since 2011, so the RBA would be taking a leap into the unknown if it goes there.

It won't want to take tens or hundreds of thousands of Australian borrowers off a mortgage cliff with it.

If it hikes in September and that proves to be a mistake, the earliest the RBA could realistically change course without totally losing face would be February.

Having moved early, it still feels to me like the RBA has bought itself time to swim against the current tide of rising interest rates for a bit longer. We'll find out soon whether the majority of its board members agree.

title: Callers told no ambulances available almost 17,000 times in Tasmania
text:
When Rosie Maddock fell over in the bathroom while at a pathology appointment, the 75-year-old did not expect to be waiting too long for medical help.

Mrs Maddock said the wait for an ambulance ended up being three hours long.

WARNING: This story contains an image of an injury some may find distressing.

"So I just lay there on the cold floor, cement floor, waiting for the ambulance to come," she told the ABC, calling it "quite painful".

" It's a dreadful thing. "

Rosie Maddock's injury was serious enough that she stayed in hospital for three weeks. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

The early May incident occurred in Glenorchy, 15 minutes from the Royal Hobart Hospital.

It was serious enough that Mrs Maddock ended up staying in hospital for three weeks, dealing with blood clots and bruising in her leg.

"My life wasn't in danger, but I don't think it helped my situation at all," she said.

Rosie Maddock suffered bruising and blood clots. (Supplied: Rosie Maddock)

Calling Triple Zero to find out there is no ambulance immediately available is becoming more and more common.

In fact, it happened nearly 17,000 times in 2025-26, or around 46 times per day.

Health department figures obtained by the Labor state opposition show the number of delayed activations (counted as taking three minutes or longer for a vehicle to be dispatched), rose 30 per cent compared to the year before.

It coincides with a 6 per cent increase in the total number of Triple Zero calls — reaching 115,735 in 2025-26.

Labor's Health spokesperson Sarah Lovell called the figures "deeply concerning".

"Tasmanians should have confidence that there is an ambulance available for them when they need it," she said.

Ramping happens when a hospital is unable to admit a patient, so that person must remain in the care of ambulance paramedics, effectively rendering the ambulance unavailable for other jobs. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

'Life or death situations' affected, paramedics union says

Health and Community Services Union state secretary Robbie Moore said the situation was "simply unacceptable".

"It's exactly what paramedic comms staff who answer the Triple Zero calls are telling us — they're saying they're unable to dispatch ambulances to people that need them," he said.

"We see ambulances unavailable for people in a life-or-death situation — that happens regularly."

He said the unavailability of ambulances was due to bed block in hospitals.

"The solutions are there — we can invest in our allied health professionals who avoid people coming to hospital and get you out of hospital sooner, we invest in more paramedics and better ambulance services," Mr Moore said.

Bridget Archer says delays may be caused by an ambulance "attending to somebody who is having a medical episode of a higher acuity". (ABC News: Jonny McNee)

Health Minister Bridget Archer pointed to the increased demand when asked about the increase in delayed dispatches.

"I want to be really clear with Tasmanians — if you call an ambulance and you need an ambulance, you will get an ambulance," she said.

She also reiterated that all Triple Zero calls were triaged according to clinical need.

" Whilst I empathise with someone who may be waiting for that ambulance to arrive, that ambulance may well be attending to somebody who is having a medical episode of a higher acuity. "

Numbers indicate 'ramping ban' ineffectual

In the 2024 state election campaign, the Liberals promised to "ban ambulance ramping" by instituting a protocol where patients were transferred from ambulances to the emergency department within a set time.

This was initially set at 60 minutes, to be lowered over time.

Ms Lovell said the figures were proof that the "ramping ban" had not worked.

The figures obtained by Labor also showed no significant improvement in the median ambulance response time in any region over the last two years.

Mr Moore said the government had "effectively withdrawn" from it, because it had been unable to implement the next stage of the protocol where there would be a 45-minute limit.

" We know every day here at the Royal [Hobart Hospital] they fail to get even 70 per cent of ambulances away within an hour. "

Ms Archer said the government was still committed to the policy.

The "ramping ban" has faced opposition from the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Foundation, which has taken the state government to the Tasmanian Industrial Commission to block its implementation.

title: 'Cinema' expected as rival wingers go to battle one last time
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Robert Toia will have a front-row seat to the last instalment of the battle between teammate Mark Nawaqanitawase and Ronaldo Mulitalo, and the Sydney Roosters centre is bracing himself for more box-office entertainment.

"Cinema, that's what I expect — [another chapter in] an ongoing battle and I think if we get the win that will top it off," Toia said.

Saturday's sudden-death semifinal could be Nawaqanitawase's last in the NRL, with the 26-year-old former Wallabies star switching back to the 15-man code with Japanese side Saitama Wild Knights.

Few could have imagined the impact Nawaqanitawase would have had in rugby league when he crossed codes after the Paris Olympics.

There have been highlights in just about every game — be it his grubber ahead and tip toe down the sideline against Canterbury last season that was named try of the year, or last weekend's tap-ahead intercept before climbing off the deck and racing away to score against Penrith.

"It's pretty hard to stay alert because you don't know what's going to happen," Toia said.

"I didn't expect him to do what he's been doing, I think he has shocked everyone."

Nawaqanitawase's long-running on-field feud with the sledge-happy Mulitalo — the pair of wingers openly admire each other off it — has made Roosters-Sharks games fixtures to savour.

"There's a bit of competitiveness there but I think that is what makes the game so great — it's the best of the best going at it with each other," said Roosters forward Siua Wong.

Toia's opposite number KL Iro said of Mulitalo: "He can get personal at times but after the game he always makes sure he clears it up straight away and shakes his hand.

"He loves getting in the mix, he's a huge competitor."

Nawaqanitawase has made the switch to rugby league look easy, having won caps for the Kangaroos, played State of Origin for NSW and scored 41 tries in 44 games for the Roosters.

The Roosters and Sharks battle on Saturday night from the Sydney Football Stadium.

title: Planning minister halts Sydney Town Hall Square project
text:
Tell us about your experience.

NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully has hit the brakes on the City of Sydney's $150 million Town Hall Square project, forcing the project to be examined by the Independent Planning Commission.

Mr Scully issued a direction to the council on Thursday, preventing it from determining development applications or demolition orders in relation to the project.

The council envisages a 4,500-square-metre civic plaza opposite Town Hall as a gathering point for community events, music events and markets.

Speaking with 702 ABC Sydney, Mr Scully said he believed it could be considered a "state significant development", given the cost of the project and the demolition of "cultural and commercially" significant buildings.

"I feel it could meet the definition of state or regional planning significance," Mr Scully said.

"I want to get that advice from the Independent Planning Commission. That's the requirement of me under the act [Environmental Planning & Assessment Act]."

Paul Scully's decision pauses work on the development of the square, which had been due for completion in 2031. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

City of Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore said she was "shocked and disappointed" by the government's decision that could delay or block the project.

"In 2025, we briefed the planning minister on the project in detail and no concerns were raised," Cr Moore said.

"The NSW government also approved the City's acquisition of the final property needed to deliver the square."

"The timing and nature of today's intervention inevitably raises questions, particularly as political attention begins to turn towards the next state election."

City of Sydney Deputy Mayor Jess Miller also criticised the decision as "disappointing", arguing the area needed more open space.

"We're going to have a huge increase of population in the city of Sydney. We're going to need new public squares," she told 702 ABC Sydney.

" It's been done very thoughtfully. We've saved up our pennies. "

Jess Miller says the decision by Paul Scully is disappointing. (Supplied: Anna Hay)

"We've done all the right things and to have the kind of state significant magic wand kind of waved over this is really awful."

Plans for the square have been on display for community feedback since early August, with artist impressions showing the open square with a water feature and a curved grove of native trees.

The council resolved in February this year to move ahead with the design and construction of the square, with a unanimous decision to fast-track demolition work of the buildings on land the city has obtained since the 1980s.

Union backs government move

The proposal has drawn opposition from the retail workers union, which argues the demolition of seven buildings, including a Woolworths supermarket, retail stores and a pub, will put 1,000 jobs at risk.

Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association NSW state secretary Bernie Smith said 300 of those jobs were in the Woolworths and Big W on the corner building.

"There's not a suitable floor space currently available to relocate that shop, as far as we are aware, that would actually preserve all of those jobs," Mr Smith said.

Bernie Smith said there were 300 jobs in the Woolworths premises between the supermarket and the Big W store. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

" Our members' jobs are potentially at risk depending on the outcome. "

Cr Miller told 702 ABC Sydney the supermarket would be able to find an alternative location "200 metres down the road".

"Of all of my sympathies, they're not being extended to one of the biggest multinational or big corporate companies," she said.

" The jobs won't disappear. "

The project was envisaged as a centre for community events and markets. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

Mr Smith hit back at Cr Miller's comments, saying the deputy mayor should "spend less time in Town Hall and maybe a bit more time in her community to realise what's really going on across the road".

Advocacy group Business Sydney head Paul Nicolaou, who opposes the plan, said the supermarket was the only full-service kind in the CBD and was "vital to the future of a city where more people are choosing to live".

"Thoughts of a Town Hall Square might have been a nice-to-have when the concept was first mooted more than 30 years ago," Mr Nicolaou said.

"But the economic realities of 2026 are very different."

Both Mr Nicolaou and Mr Smith supported the government's move to have it assessed by the planning commission.

title: Canberra is the greatest mystery of the NRLW finals
text:
Of all the teams in the fight for the NRLW premiership, Canberra shapes as the ultimate wildcard.

Ahead of the first finals series in club history, the Raiders are a difficult puzzle to solve; for themselves and opponents alike.

Darrin Borthwick's side enter the finals in fifth place with a 6-5 record that belies a strange tendency that developed over the season: more than any other team in the league, they play to their opponent's level.

Can anyone stop the Roosters in the NRLW? After completing the most dominant regular season in NRLW history, the big question around the Sydney Roosters is simple: can anyone hope to stop them?

The Raiders have a winning record against fellow top six teams, highlighted by a 28-4 win over third-placed Broncos, comfortably the Brisbane team's biggest ever NRLW loss.

They even put the gloves up against powerhouses Gold Coast and Sydney Roosters, losing to the two competition heavyweights by a combined 10 points, finishing close enough in both games that they would fancy their chances in a rematch.

But as easily as the Raiders can be inspired by the challenge of taking on the big dogs, they can be complacent when facing teams they should handle easily.

Canberra dropped games to stragglers Parramatta, North Queensland and Cronulla throughout the season, costing them a home final.

As they prepare to head to Campbelltown to take on Wests Tigers in tomorrow night's sudden-death final, they are still trying to work themselves out as they head into the deep waters.

"I've found we've lifted for those bigger teams. We've spoken about that, that we need to believe we can win because if we get that down, our effort and our fight will come," said captain Zahara Temara.

"For some of the other teams who aren't as high on the ladder, we've matched them in terms of effort, and that's disappointing. But we know we can lift for the big teams."

It is an unorthodox way for Canberra to live, but now that only big teams are left, the Raiders' record against the top sides makes them perhaps the best candidate to break open the Roosters-Titans hegemony at the top.

Canberra will lean heavily on Zahara Temara's experience through the finals. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Temara's experience will be crucial for Canberra, with the clever halfback one of the few Raiders with an extensive finals pedigree, having won a premiership with the Roosters in 2022.

That was the 29-year-old's third grand final, and she admits she took the team's success for granted in the earlier years, something she is desperate to ensure does not happen to her Raiders teammates this time around.

"Something I wish someone told me in those early years at the Roosters was how hard it is to have regrets. I took it seriously, but not as seriously as I could have," said Temara.

"It's hard to make the finals. It's extremely hard to win a grand final, and with the position we're in now, I want them to have no regrets, to realise how we can make history."

That perspective was reinforced by former Roosters teammate and current Canberra co-captain Simaima Taufa, especially after their losing effort in the 2020 grand final.

The Raiders will be without gun lock forward Simaima Taufa tomorrow night. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The sight of the whole-hearted Taufa after the match has never left Temara, and inspires her to this day.

"She gave it her everything, and I didn't feel like I did," said Temara.

"We were all disappointed, but I tell her all the time now I couldn't look at her because I knew I hadn't done everything I could for her and the team.

"I still took it seriously. I just wish I took it as far as she did."

With Taufa sidelined due to suspension, there will be even more responsibility on Temara's shoulders tomorrow night.

The Tigers are polar opposites of the Raiders: they beat every side that missed the finals, but went 1-4 against the other play-off teams, with their sole success coming via a one-point win over Newcastle.

But there are similarities too. The joint venture is also playing in its first finals match, and given Raecene McGregor's form at halfback, the team will also lean heavily on an experienced playmaker to show the way.

Inside Tigers remarkable NRLW turnaround Few expected much from Wests Tigers in this year's NRLW competition, but after winning as many games this season as the rest of their history combined they've proved the doubters wrong ahead of a maiden finals push.

To add to the intrigue, this is a rematch only seven days in the making. The two sides met last Friday night at Leichhardt with the Raiders grinding out a 22-10 victory.

Winger Mackenzie Wiki and centre Leianne Tufuga, who was crowned the club's player of the year, both played blinders as Canberra's strike out wide carried the day.

It ensured the Tigers would enter the finals on the back of consecutive losses, but Temara understands how dangerous they still can be when the stakes are highest.

"Their fight stood out," said Temara

"They were down on the scoreboard, but their fight and hunger to keep coming at us was hard to manage. We got lucky with some errors and penalties that kept the momentum for us."

title: These women were married for decades before learning their husbands were gay
text:
Karen's husband was working from home one day when she noticed something strange on his laptop.

"As I walked past, something jumped out at me, so I looked," says the now 59-year-old from Melbourne/Naarm.

"Open on the computer were sort of all these gay [adult websites], and my heart sank; I was like 'What is this?'"

It was the beginning of a very painful period where Karen's marriage of two decades fell apart with her husband's eventual admission that he was gay.

"It was very, very difficult, he went into a massive shame spiral," she says.

"He hated that part of himself and couldn't reconcile it, he had married me hoping it would go away.

"I remember leaving the house for the day and I just sat in the car and just cried."

Karen is not alone in her experience. Yumi Stynes, host of ABC podcast Ladies, We Need to Talk, spoke with women about the shock of finding out their husband's sexuality and how they moved on to find peace.

'This is who I am'

Annie, a mother of two from Victoria, discovered her husband's sexuality after she became unwell.

"I'd had sort of stomach cramps and sort of an ongoing period that wouldn't go away," says 49-year-old Annie, not her real name.

"I went to the GP, and she did some swabs and tests and she goes, 'Oh, you've actually got chlamydia'.

Women 'quiet quitting' relationships Some women are doing only the bare minimum in their romantic relationships.

"So, I rang my husband while I was in the [doctor's] room, and I said, 'Have you been playing around?' And he said, 'Yes, but not with women.'"

Annie says she felt disgusted and deceived by her husband.

"I said to him, 'You're going for counselling, and you need to work out whether you're gay or bisexual and if this is just a phase'.

"I didn't want to tell our children until I knew where he was at.

"He was able to identify, 'No, this is not just a phase, this is who I am.'"

'I didn't sign up for this'

Karen says her husband's shame around his identity made her feel like she was "in the closet with him".

"He wanted to know whether I was going to stick it out, and he was terrified that I would leave, I was a cover.

"I got to a point of really realising it wasn't fair to either of us, and that we both deserved to be free.

"After 15 months of cohabiting with this dark secret, he eventually agreed that the kids did have a right to know, we had this dinner, and it felt like the Last Supper."

Karen says she felt "invisible" when her husband's sexuality was revealed. (Supplied)

Karen says when he eventually told close family and friends, they were all happy for him, but she felt "invisible and overlooked".

"I couldn't say, 'This is awful. My life is really difficult,' because by doing that, it seemed defamatory to this person who's coming out.

"I do think he cared for me, but I feel used, and I feel that collateral damage is really painful.

" I didn't sign up for this, and if I had known, I would've said no. "

Annie says she and her husband lived together for a year after he came out, and she found it difficult to let him go emotionally.

"Some people were saying, 'Annie, it's OK. You can be upset and angry.'

"But that only really came later, in the last probably three years, that fact that I am collateral."

Finding a place of peace

Both women say it has taken some time for them to move past the hurt and betrayal to find peace.

Karen says she has come to accept the injustice of her marriage, while building her own happiness.

" I have learnt to love myself, I'm not just a gay guy's wife, I'm much more … so much more. "

She says her healing journey has involved "reinventing" herself.

"So, I went from full-time mothering to full-time uni and poured myself into that and haven't looked back."

Annie says connecting with others who've gone through similar experiences has been helpful. She says she was also able attended the wedding of her ex-husband and his new partner.

"I'm still rebuilding what life looks like and I do see my ex-husband, who's got an amazing partner and we get on well considering everything.

"I am an optimist, and I just think life's too short to hold grudges.

"I want women to know that it's OK, and it's actually more common than people think."

title: Iraqi Australians behind 'promising' type 1 diabetes treatment research
text:
Tell us about your experience.

A Far North Queensland couple who started their research journey in Cairns are behind "promising" early research on a new type 1 diabetes treatment.

Rafid Al-Hallaf and his wife, Zainab Agha, migrated to Cairns in 2013 to study immunology at James Cook University (JCU).

More than a decade later, they are part of new research published in the Journal of Immunology from Johns Hopkins University (JHU) in America targeting type 1 diabetes.

According to Diabetes Australia, about 134,000 Australians are currently living with type 1 diabetes, an autoimmune condition.

Dr Al-Hallaf says trial results were really promising. (Supplied: Rafid Al-Hallaf)

Current treatment replaces the insulin that the body can no longer make.

"Our approach is different because we are trying to treat the cause of the disease, which is the autoimmune attack," Dr Al-Hallaf said.

"Rather than simply replacing the insulin, we are trying to stop the immune system from destroying the cell that produces it."

What did they discover?

During an immune response like diabetes, the immune system produces a variety of antibodies, including some that scientists do not fully understand.

JHU scientists, led by Abdel-Rahim Hamad, found immune cells from type 1 diabetes patients were making a specific, previously unrecognised antibody, dubbed "x-mAb".

Dr Hamad said current immunotherapy treatment worked "like a sledgehammer", suppressing large parts of the immune system and leaving patients vulnerable to infections.

The things people with diabetes want you to be aware of We spoke to six people with three different types of diabetes to find out what they wish more of the public knew. Here's what they had to say.

However, he said the x-mAb antibody worked like a "guided missile".

"It selectively disarms only the rogue T cells destroying the pancreas, leaving the rest of your immune defence fully functional."

In a trial on mice in the early stages of type 1 diabetes, 16 were treated with the antibody and five with a placebo.

All 16 mice had their blood sugar return to normal levels, while none of the placebo mice went into remission.

Abdel-Rahim Hamad first discovered the novel immune cell that has catalysed the x-mAb research. (Supplied: Johns Hopkins University)

In another experiment of pre-diabetic mice, 10 received the antibody and 10 received a placebo.

About 70 per cent of those treated mice then stayed disease-free for the rest of the three-month study.

"This is really, really promising," Dr Al-Hallaf said.

'Holy grail' of treatment

St Vincent's Institute immunologist Tom Kay, who is not involved in the research, said it had promising results.

"It's a creative and out-of-left-field idea that I think brings new ideas to the field," Professor Kay said.

Tom Kay says the research is promising. (Supplied: Thomas Kay)

He said scientists had long chased precisely that kind of highly targeted treatment.

"It's a holy grail in treating autoimmunity that you're trying to make the treatment as specific as possible," he said.

Professor Kay said the earlier a patient was treated after diagnosis, the more of their own insulin production could be preserved.

His own team had worked on identifying a key driver of the autoimmune attack in type 1 diabetes and trialled an existing rheumatoid arthritis drug, baricitinib, in newly diagnosed patients.

Unlike x-mAb, which aims to precisely target only the specific rogue immune cells, the St Vincent's Institute's drug blocked the whole immune-signalling pathway driving the disease.

However, Professor Kay said there were limitations in how short the JHU mouse trials were and he would have liked to see them carried out longer to see if the drug had a lasting impact.

The research shows "promising" results in preventing the onset of diabetes in pre-diabetic mice. (Supplied: Johns Hopkins University)

He said he would closely watch the research as it moved from mice towards possible human trials.

To undertake human trials, the JHU team will first need clearance from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

"You're talking about definitely a decade, probably more, to go from successful mouse studies to the end of clinical trials," Professor Kay said.

Home in Cairns

As the research moves forward, Dr Al-Hallaf said his family ultimately wanted to return to Cairns where they still own a home.

He hopes the JHU discovery could help treat skin cancer in Far North Queensland, where some of the highest rates occur.

The researchers say the antibody can target the rogue immune cells like a "guided missile". (Supplied: Rafid Al-Hallaf)

"We want to further characterise these cells … to see if this antibody can also have an impact on animals that have cancer," he said.

title: Newly minted Bluey Dollarbuck features beloved backyard cricketer
text:
Tell us about your experience.

"Are you right with a bit of spin, Rusty?" Bluey's dad, Bandit, asks as one of his daughter's mates steps up to the crease.

"All good, Mr Heeler," Rusty replies, cricket bat at the ready.

That much-loved scene from an episode of the ABC children's cartoon Bluey has played in households worldwide, and will now appear on a $1 coin.

And like all Bluey episodes, there are life lessons to be found in season three's Cricket, where Rusty's dad pens a letter to his son from military deployment:

"I wish I could be there to bowl a few at you, but I can't right now, mate. But look, as you grow up, you'll face harder things than a cricket ball, and you'll have two choices," the letter read.

"Back away and get out, or step in front and play a full shot. Just keep your eye on the ball and take care of your little sister for me," Rusty's dad wrote.

Rusty in the Bluey episode, Cricket. (ABC)

Second round of Dollarbucks

The Royal Australian Mint's new $1 coin, which will not be circulated but is available for collecting, shows Rusty hitting the ball as Bluey cheers in the background.

Mint chief executive Emily Martin said the choice to create a new Bluey coin came down to Australia's love of cricket and the children's series.

The Mint's CEO says the new coloured coin "brings together the fun of cricket with the heart and humour of Bluey". (Supplied: The Royal Australian Mint)

"This colourful coin brings together the fun of cricket with the heart and humour of Bluey, celebrating the friendships, teamwork and memories that make playing together so special," Ms Martin said.

" Cricket is a little bit like life — sometimes you hit a six, sometimes you miss the ball completely, and sometimes your little sister insists she's not out. "

This isn't the first time the Mint has used Bluey's popularity to get younger people into coin collecting.

The Mint released coins featuring the blue heeler two years ago.

The 2024 Bluey Dollarbucks were a collection of three colourful coins featuring Bluey on her own, the Heeler family together, and Bingo and Bluey dressed up as The Grannies.

The latest release will mint 200,000 uncirculated coloured Bluey coins and an additional 20,000 silver proof coins.

title: Olympic authorities sign off on controversial rowing and canoeing venue
text:
Tell us about your experience.

After months of fierce debate, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) has approved rowing and canoe sprint events on Rockhampton's Fitzroy River for the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Premier David Crisafulli said the doubters had been proven wrong with today's announcement.

"The IOC assessment for the site is complete," Mr Crisafulli said.

" The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours. It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered. "

International rowing bodies had questioned the location's suitability for competition. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

It comes after World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide also backed an independent technical assessment of the Rockhampton flatwater course.

The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) and internationally renowned marine engineering experts WaterProof Marine Consultancy and Services B.V. (WaterProof) completed a comprehensive, independent technical assessment of the Fitzroy River.

The assessment included extensive on-water investigations and modelling to understand how the course would perform under a range of conditions, weather patterns, water levels and flood risk at both Games time and throughout the period leading into the event.

The assessment included detailed surveys of the riverbed and competition course. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Having reviewed the assessment, World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland and Paddle Worldwide president Thomas Konietzko endorsed the central Queensland waterway.

Mr Rolland said it could provide a safe, fair and consistent field of play suitable for Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoe sprint competitions.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic rowing," he said.

A future Olympic dream is taking shape on the Fitzroy River, where young rowers could one day compete for their country on their hometown course. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleije told state parliament "it's a win for regional Queensland".

"The experts have confirmed it. World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide have endorsed it," he said.

" Rockhampton is good for rowing and rowing is good for 2032 and beyond. "

Now the decision is confirmed, Paddle Australia president and triple Olympian Andrew Trim said the national body was "excited to work with all our athletes, current and emerging, to maximise this once in a lifetime opportunity to compete at the biggest sporting event in the world on home soil".

Rowing Australia has been contacted for comment.

Game on Rocky

Tony Williams has thanked the state government for its support of Olympic rowing in the city. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Rockhampton Mayor Tony Williams welcomed the confirmation of the Fitzroy River as the venue for rowing at the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

"This endorsement proves what we've always known. That Rockhampton's Fitzroy River will be the perfect venue for rowing at the 2032 Games," he said.

"Rockhampton is ready for the world stage. Now it's time to get to work and secure the infrastructure and opportunities that will benefit our community long after the Games have ended."

Queensland senator and National Party leader Matt Canavan, who first championed the Fitzroy River as an Olympic venue, said it was a great day for central Queensland.

The Fitzroy River has faced intense scrutiny since it was selected as a venue for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

"The Fitzroy River is one of the most beautiful parts of our country. It's an iconic Australian river," he said.

" It's been a tough fight, and some people had not wanted rowing to be outside of south-east Queensland. "

The Queensland premier said GIICA would now proceed with the detailed planning, design and construction of the Rockhampton site.

He also told state parliament there would be no widening or dredging and that the Fitzroy Barrage was Rockhampton's "secret weapon".

The Rockhampton rowing facility will host the Queensland Schools' Championship regatta this weekend. (Supplied: Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club)

While the river has passed an independent technical assessment, the region will require more accommodation to support an influx of athletes and visitors in 2032.

"Rockhampton knows how to host major events. It already hosts tens of thousands of people for Beef Week and Rockynats, and the Games will deliver extra accommodation for the future," Mr Crisafulli said.

Rowing Queensland chief executive Anthea O'Loughlin also welcomed the outcome of the technical assessment, as the Rockhampton venue prepared to host more than 800 young rowers for the Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta this weekend.

"This is an important step to provide certainty to our athletes and community as we progress towards 2032," Ms O'Loughlin said.

"We note the references in the statement to legacy and investment in the sport and look forward to further information on this as it develops."

Sarah Black says the Olympics will bring a great legacy. (ABC Capricornia: Katrina Beavan)

President of the Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club, Sarah Black, was ecstatic when the ABC broke the news to her that Rockhampton had been given the final seal of approval from the IOC.

"We've known that the course here is fantastic, but to have that international endorsement for the technical assessment is just fantastic news for us here in Rockhampton," she said.

Capricorn Enterprise chief executive Mary Carroll said today's announcement was a major milestone for central Queensland and an opportunity to deliver lasting economic, tourism and community benefits for the region.

"Commercial in confidence discussions have been proceeding positively with major investors to this region who I strongly believe will be able to deliver new hotel accommodation, an athletes' village and legacy infrastructure including world-class rowing and canoeing facilities," she said.

title: New laws on mining objections 'hacking at safety net'
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Queensland communities could find it harder to challenge new mining projects under proposed laws that would restrict who can object to a mine and give politicians greater control over whether objections are heard in court.

Resources Minister Dale Last introduced the Mineral Resources Objections Reform and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2026 on Tuesday, arguing the changes would cut red tape and stop "vexatious" objections from holding up projects.

Dale Last says the bill will put a stop to "vexatious claims". (ABC Rural: Brandon Long)

But farmers, environmental groups and lawyers said the reforms would instead make it harder for communities to have their say and weaken independent scrutiny of mines.

Under the proposed laws, objections would generally be restricted to landholders directly affected by a project and others living within 125 kilometres of a proposed mine.

Automatic referrals of objections to the Land Court would also disappear, with decisions about whether an objection went to court instead made through "a ministerial referral process".

'Benefit from an open process'

Barrister and University of Queensland adjunct professor Chris McGrath said the changes would undermine the approvals system.

"This is another step of this current government in really hacking at the safety net of laws that protect Queenslanders from bad development," Dr McGrath said.

"We all benefit from an open process with independent review, and they're really blowing holes in that process."

Under the proposed laws, objections would generally be restricted to landholders directly affected by a project and others living within 125 kilometres of a proposed mine. (Supplied: Ernest Henry)

Dr McGrath said the proposed 125km limit failed to recognise that the effects of a mine could travel far beyond its immediate footprint.

But mining industry group Queensland Resources Council chief executive Janette Hewson argued the 125km limit is an "arbitrary number".

She said the government uses different radii for different impacts, such as groundwater and air emissions.

"We think that it should be more of a sliding scale that's actually based on science and data."

Janette Hewson says people are fighting approvals on ideologies "really not relevant" to the issue. (Supplied: Queensland Resources Council)

Dr McGrath said the reforms could also restrict the ability of incorporated community groups to bring objections to the Land Court.

He said those groups had played an important role in protecting landholders during the long-running New Acland mine expansion battle on Queensland's Darling Downs.

He represented landowners involved with the Oakey Coal Action Alliance (OCAA), which challenged the expansion that was later approved.

Dr McGrath said incorporated groups such as OCAA could also provide landholders with protection against potentially significant legal costs.

OCAA president and Brymaroo dairy farmer David Vonhoff, who lives 6km from the mine, described the proposed changes as "very disturbing".

"The mining people … dictate terms to the government and the government's just listening to them and not listening to the people that are producing the food on the land," he said.

Mr Vonhoff questioned why people who lived further away should be excluded from the process if they had legitimate concerns about a project.

Mr Last said the bill would streamline the objections process without reducing environmental protections.

"[It's] to deliver a more efficient and targeted framework for objections to mining lease applications while putting a stop to those who lob vexatious claims and intentionally use this process to frustrate or delay project approvals," the minister said.

He said the existing system had left projects such as New Acland without certainty for almost 15 years.

Dale Last says the bill will streamline processes without reducing environmental protections. (Supplied: Arlie Felton-Taylor)

Ms Hewson said, for the mining industry, this was about cutting duplicated red tape.

"It's not about taking people's rights away," she said.

Ms Hewson said they were also seeing activists fighting approvals on ideologies "really not relevant" to the issue.

"Where objections are made … about a project simply for ideological reasons such as climate change."

The bill is the latest in a series of changes by the government aimed at accelerating resource and major-project approvals.

In June, the government launched a review of Queensland's mining rehabilitation financial safeguards.

Then in August, parliament passed critical-minerals laws giving the government new powers to fast-track projects declared "state strategic".

The government has also shown it can retreat from proposed changes, abandoning plans to remove a key approval protecting farmland and groundwater.

The new mining objections bill will now be debated by Queensland parliament.

title: Greene to leave Giants ahead of expected move to Cats

The GWS Giants have confirmed Toby Greene will leave the club to potentially join Geelong ahead of the 2027 season.

Greene has told the Cats he wants to join the club from next season.

Toby Greene (second from right) was a foundation player at the Giants. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Mark Kolbe)

Greene can join the Cats as an unrestricted free agent once the free agency period opens on October 2.

"We are really excited Toby wants to join the Geelong Football Club," Cats executive general manager of football, Andrew Mackie, said in a statement.

"We know this was a significant decision for Toby and his family, and we recognise what the Giants have meant to him and respect the contribution he has made to their club.

"We are looking forward to helping Toby write the next chapter of his career at the Cats."

Last week, Greene spoke about his talks with the Cats.

"With Geelong, I've had an open discussion," Greene said last week.

"Told them what I think about and what I wrestle with and they then explained what it would look like for me.

He nominated him for the $1 million group 2 Shorts over 1200m but opted for the easier task in the last, a benchmark 88 handicap over 1100m.

“He raced a fraction flat,” Pfieffer said of the most recent run. “I know he was three deep, but he’d get away with that in the past, although I know you can’t keep doing that as you go up in grade. “I think he appreciates being kept that bit fresh and obviously being up on pace, but just these little things he does wrong are signs of immaturity and a lot of it comes down to him being a boy in a man’s game. “For now, we’ll just take these baby steps while he’s developing his trade. Even just stepping slow from the gates, it’s just little things he’s doing wrong that aren’t helping him. “But I thought his trial was super. He stepped away from the gates nice, put himself on pace, travelled along at a comfortable tempo without overdoing it. He ran good sectionals without asking a lot of him.

Advertisement

“And his coat, I think come Saturday, it will be the best he’s looked his whole career, and like the old saying goes, when they look good, they race well.” Pfieffer has long planned to test Ice Kool, a $3.80 chance on Saturday, on the straight courses in Melbourne over the spring carnival and he was eyeing the group 2 Schillaci Stakes (1100m) on October 10 at Caulfield. “Getting some experience down at Melbourne will do him good and, let’s be honest, he doesn’t need to be taking on these sprinters heading to the Everest, unless he comes out and blows them away on Saturday,” he said. “Then you might rethink and go, do we throw him in the Premiere? But at this stage, you are taking the safer play.” At Newcastle on Friday, Pfieffer has Oh Diamond Lil ($4) from gate one in the group 3 Tibbie Stakes. She was sixth first-up in the Mona Lisa Stakes.

Advertisement

“She was three deep for a bit then she had to push across and get to the front,” he said. “I just don’t think she got that mid-race breather, and being a six-year-old mare now, she’s probably holding a bit more condition and the fitter horses had her covered. “She wasn’t beaten far, her sectionals were still strong. They went five lengths above average mid-race, so that’s going to test a lot of horses out first-up. She’s come out of it well.”

title: Absurd and exciting, this surreal romp will keep you entertained
text:
Advertisement

Key points DANCE: Harrison Ritchie-Jones and Michaela Tancheff perform R.A.I.N at Arts House

MUSIC: Belle and Sebastian return to the Palais with If You’re Feeling Sinister

MUSIC: Cellist Pieter Wispelwey explores solo suites by Benjamin Britten

DANCE: Hobart’s Nelipot Collective bring Our Last Tree to La Mama

OPERA: Lyric Opera put on a Regency-Era Serse at the Gasworks Theatre

DANCE

R.A.I.N ★★★★

Arts House, North Melbourne, until September 20 There’s nothing quite like the shared movement language of Harrison Ritchie-Jones and Michaela Tancheff. Their vocabulary of sporty grappling and mutual manipulation, first seen several years ago in the excellent Cuddle, combines rough-handling with exquisite responsiveness and apparent sensitivity. Harrison Ritchie-Jones and Michaela Tancheff in a scene from R.A.I.N. Darren Gill The opening section of their latest collaboration has playful echoes of a ballroom routine. Extravagant lifts and twists and shifts of momentum also suggest a wrestling contest, with each dancer constantly tracing the other’s body to maintain contact, seeking ways to connect their repertoire of moves. As in Cuddle, they keep up a murmured dialogue, discussing their options and deciding what comes next. Moves are named like invitations which can be accepted or rejected. These casual exchanges make the choreography seem negotiated live: an intricate physical conversation with its own laconic commentary.

Advertisement

Paradoxically, this verbal back and forth makes us more aware of who initiates and who responds, inviting us to diagnose power relations in the mechanics of partnering. Or, at the very least, it draws attention to the contrast in their stage personalities: one expansive and eager, the other more reserved and reactive. Structurally, the development of the show from scene to scene feels a little arbitrary. Of course, the unexpected twists and turns are part of the fun, but I think I would have enjoyed this show even more if there was a clearer sense of narrative progress. The casual exchanges in R.A.I.N make the choreography seem negotiated live. Darren Gill Ritchie-Jones’s program statement describes pushing their partnering practice to its limits and exploring how it fails. But what are the stakes? Does apparent failure count as success for the performers, or is the other way around? It sounds a little too much like navel gazing. Fortunately, the absurdities of this surreal romp are sufficiently entertaining: horse-riding antics, a sudden mystifying leap into opera, crazy costumes and multiple unexpected bursts of song. There’s more than enough excitement at the surface to keep us from looking deeper.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

MUSIC

Belle and Sebastian ★★★★★

Palais Theatre, September 12 “Welcome to the second recording session for this still quite-new band,” Stuart Murdoch says with a grin. His tongue is firmly in cheek – Belle and Sebastian, the indie-pop group he’s led for more than half his life, is on tour celebrating its 30th year. In 1996, the bookish Scots made their debut with two albums: Tigermilk and If You’re Feeling Sinister. On this anniversary tour, they’re alternating playing those records in full. Melbourne gets the Sinister treatment. Belle & Sebastian perform at the Palais, September 12, 2026. Richard Clifford Playing albums in full live can be a cynical cash-cow in the age of commodified nostalgia, but there’s no denying the sheer delight of hearing a beloved album like this in all its glory. On record, Sinister’s arrangements are delicate; live, they’re injected with a shot of joyous energy, with buzzing synth to boot. Many of these songs begin with Murdoch alone, singing with that sweet, instantly recognisable voice, before the eight other musicians on stage slowly blossom to create sunlight in musical form. Lead guitarist Stevie Jackson raucously takes on the harmonica for Me and the Major, his movements a chaotic blur.

Advertisement

As the album reaches its halfway point, a projection behind the band shows the LP being flipped on a turntable – “a bit of antiquated attention to detail,” Murdoch says. Eager fans have been dancing in the aisles from the beginning, but when the band plays Get Me Away, I’m Dying, the entire venue is on its feet. The gorgeous Mayfly is another highlight from this half, but really, it’s all joy, not least because Murdoch and co are clearly having a blast, too. Murdoch’s signature humour is on display all night as he intersperses the music with quips, including a spiel about Victoria’s slogans as seen on number plates and a joke about Viagra as he takes his medication on stage. “Back to sweetness and light!” he says, and back they go. Sarah Martin, Stuart Murdoch and Stevie Jackson of Belle & Sebastian. Richard Clifford A guitar-heavy I’m a Cuckoo kicks off the second set, comprising songs from the rest of the band’s long career. Belle and Sebastian have such a varied discography that it’s a grab-bag every night. There are some deeper cuts here, such as 2010’s Little Lou, Ugly Jack, Prophet John, recorded with Norah Jones; here, it’s long-time vocalist Sarah Martin who does the honours, beautiful as ever. 2006’s Funny Little Frog is a charming, nostalgic treat. The band is pulling songs out on the fly by the end, with Another Sunny Day closing the night. It’s apt – with 30 years of sunny days up their sleeves, Belle and Sebastian keep on delivering.

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

MUSIC

Pieter Wispelwey with Piers Lane ★★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, September 15 Pure genius. These two words arguably encapsulate the astonishing imagination behind the three solo suites that Benjamin Britten composed for the Russian cellist Mstislav Rostropovich between 1964 and 1971. Taking Bach’s fabled cello suites as a model, these tours de force remain revolutionary in pushing the instrument’s boundaries of timbre and texture. Pieter Wispelwey performs at Melbourne Recital Centre, September 15, 2026 Laura Manariti Over three evenings, Dutch cellist Pieter Wispelwey, long an ardent and persuasive exponent of these works, is performing programs centred around each suite. Prokofiev and Shostakovich were appropriate stablemates in the series opener, not least because Prokofiev wrote his Cello Sonata in C, Op. 119 for Rostropovich, but also that the cellist was part of the deep friendship and admiration shared between himself, Shostakovich and Britten.

Advertisement

Providing the first taste of Wispelwey’s chameleonic way with his 1760 Guadagnini cello, the Prokofiev ran the gamut of emotions, starting with its dark, sombre opening before flowering into rich lyricism, moments of childlike wonder and folkloric exuberance. Britten’s Cello Suite No. 1, Op. 72 was full of ear-bending marvels, including a witty, cleverly constructed fugue and an evocative march in which the masterly bouncing of the bow summoned up martial images. A stunning moto perpetuo led to the return of the imposing, unifying Canto. Few others would be capable of bringing this music alive so vibrantly and comprehensibly. Pianist Piers Lane’s committed partnership was entirely empathetic Laura Manariti Wispelwey ensured Shostakovich’s Cello Sonata in D minor, Op. 40 brimmed over with fascinating detail; bringing richly burnished tone to the eerie opening melody and plaintive Largo, unerring technique to the manic second movement and cheeky playfulness to the finale. Here and in the Prokofiev, pianist Piers Lane’s committed partnership was entirely empathetic. Setting aside the substandard printed program that doesn’t even list the movements of the works performed, don’t miss the remaining two opportunities to hear astounding music performed by musicians of genius.

Reviewed by Tony Way

Advertisement

DANCE

Our Last Tree ★★★

La Mama, until September 18 Hobart’s Nelipot Collective bring something we rarely see on Melbourne stages: unpretentiously referential contemporary dance. Their latest show, Our Last Tree, points us with a sort of guileless enthusiasm towards the green earth and its wonders. Nelipot Collective perform Our Last Tree as part of La Mama’s Hope Punk Climate Festival Darren Gill Sometimes the relentless self-reflexivity of our local choreographers – their unwillingness to make work about the world beyond the stage – can seem like a fear of artistic failure. Nelipot embrace that fear with an earnest, wilfully naive fable of loss and recovery. Certainly, their slightly manic smiles and touchy-feely involvement of the audience suggest a community-oriented performance. You can imagine them at a farmers’ market, amid haybales and squealing children munching on small-batch fudge.

Advertisement

And yet I find their evocation of the life of the forest compelling. What they do best here is suggest – with reaching, serpentine limbs – the way that forests envelop us completely, above and below and all around. The intimate stage at La Mama, further compressed by the placement of a cardboard tree along one side, suits these densely convolved bodies. They seem to fill the space completely, coiling themselves into any chink of vacancy. Composer and violist Andrea Breen accompanies the performance with catchy, rather grand melodic hooks, which she returns to between wandering passages. Her music suggests something rooted yet inexorably moving, a tree’s stillness alive with change. Her score also implies a fuller orchestration: I hear the ghosts of horns and oboes underneath it. And yet the exposed solo voice suggests kinship with the last tree. Haunting, effective and beautifully played. Other production elements are less impressive. The slime-green tulle and the cardboard trunk (endearingly ornamented with hand-drawn growth rings) suggest a production for children; I suspect a younger audience would respond well. Yes, the work could be called unsophisticated, but only if that also means a refreshing independence from convention, as well as the courage to approach their subject directly.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

OPERA

Serse ★★

Gasworks Theatre, until September 13 We’re all getting restless. Twenty minutes after the curtain was meant to go up for the opening show of Lyric Opera’s Serse, we’re still waiting for the conductor to raise his baton. Eventually, company artistic director and conductor Patrick Burns addresses the audience, explaining that though they’ve tried to fix the issue, they’ve had no success. Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne Jodie Hutchinson Both projectors have died. For the near-three-hour Italian opera we’re about to witness, there will be no surtitles. No translations. Oh dear. Turns out, if it was sung in English, it’d be hard to follow anyway. Handel’s 1738 opera about the King of Persia is one of those operas stacked with couples pursuing, deceiving, rejecting and reuniting with one another, plus disguises and mistaken identities thrown in, of course.

Advertisement

Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne, but for a company that has commendably programmed contemporary operas in previous seasons, Serse is, frankly, an odd choice. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever, updated to the Regency era where it fits quite well, what with all the letter-writing and love-in-turmoil. But even with tech issues aside, faults remain. The ornamentation demands were too much for some, and the approach (though it is correct Baroque style) of leaving out vibrato resulted in some unenergised vocal patches. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever. Jodie Hutchinson Some shined, like mezzo Naomi Flatman, who with a honeyed, resonant sound, delivered the standout performance of the night. Soprano Rebecca Rashleigh too gave a consistently vibrant performance, with thrilling top notes. As Serse, it was testament to Sally-Anne Russell’s comedic talent that though we mostly had no idea what was going on, people still laughed when they were, presumably, meant to. Though it was the initial problem, the ensuing convoluted plot, repetitive musical style and uneven singing proved that being sung in a foreign language is not the greatest measure of an opera’s accessibility.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

DANCE

7 Dances for 7 People ★★★

Northcote Town Hall, until September 19 Yes, there are indeed seven dances – or sections – in choreographer Trá Mi Dinh’s latest work, but only the first of them is unambiguously successful. I would happily have watched this strange, lustrous gambit for the full hour, either extended or simply repeated. Tra Mi Dinh and Rachel Coulson in 7 Dances for 7 People. Darren Gill Two dancers emerge from billowing clouds of smoke, like figures in a dream, amid an eerie tintinnabulation. Delicate unison stepping gives their progress toward the audience an insect-like grace; raised arms and joined hands further heighten their otherworldly appearance. The awkward position of the arms, which restricts the movement of the upper body, creates a sense of fragility and risk. It’s as if their grip on one another is all that prevents them tumbling back in the cloud of smoke. It gives the whole scene a shimmery, slippery sort of ephemerality.

Advertisement

After the first dance, the movement becomes more eclectic. Smooth isolations, with their tensing and releasing, give way to looser spinning figures. Vaguely balletic poses contrast with thrusting modern dance gestures. And everything whirls together in the smoke. The combinations are not always compelling, but something of the mysterious atmosphere of the first section persists. And interesting details register throughout, particularly in the way the seven dancers move between pairs and trios, with new arrangement materialising in the gloom. The balletic poses contrast with modern dance gestures as everything whirls together amid the smoke. Darren Gill This show is based on a shorter commission for Lucy Guerin’s Pieces in 2024, and it retains the same production team, including lighting designer Rachel Rui Qian Lee and costume designer Geoffrey Watson, who provides beautiful filmy smocks. Tilman Robinson’s score feels a little too insistent. The opening section with its bells has an attractive alienness, but I think the heavier beats used thereafter impose too much on the choreography and a more ambient soundscape might have been more effective.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Updated

Arts Second strike planned by Arts Centre Melbourne employees The work is apparently based on the significance of the number seven across religions and cultural traditions. Yet it is strongest when there is no theme: just fleeting relations between bodies – repetitions and doublings, divergences and singularities – in a world before number settles into meaning.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

title: Ed Sheeran rarely talks politics. The Macklemore controversy has put him at the centre of it
text:
IN BRIEF Sheeran says his concerts aren't a "political forum", but the Macklemore fallout has put that position under scrutiny.

What began with Macklemore saying "Free Palestine" on stage has grown into a wider dispute involving several artists.

Ed Sheeran has built one of the world's biggest music careers while largely avoiding one of the more divisive parts of modern celebrity: politics.

The English singer has spoken publicly about some causes over the years, including performing at a major benefit concert for Ukraine following Russia's 2022 invasion. But he has generally resisted using his concerts as a political platform, something he says is deliberate.

Now, Macklemore's removal from his United States tour has drawn Sheeran into a political debate he has largely sought to avoid.

In less than two weeks, Macklemore has made a high-profile pro-Palestinian speech while opening for Sheeran, been removed from his remaining US tour dates, and been followed out the door by four other acts.

Sheeran has insisted the decision to remove the American rapper wasn't his and says he spent days trying to prevent it.

But the fallout has nevertheless dragged the 35-year-old singer into a highly charged debate over the Israel-Gaza conflict, antisemitism and the role, or responsibility, of artists to use their platforms to take a political stand.

And it has forced Sheeran to publicly explain why, unlike Macklemore, he generally chooses not to.

"I have my personal views on this devastating conflict," Sheeran wrote in a lengthy statement posted to Instagram this week.

"Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care."

Embroiled in the controversy

The dispute began on 4 September, when Macklemore was performing as a support act on Sheeran's Loop Tour at a New Jersey stadium.

Introducing his 2024 protest song Hind's Hall, the rapper told the crowd that part of the reason he wanted to join the tour was to use its enormous stadium audiences to amplify his support for Palestinians.

"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine'," Macklemore said.

The following day, he again addressed the conflict, telling Jewish members of the audience that his criticism of Israel was not criticism of them.

The remarks sparked a backlash, with the Israeli-American Council launching a petition calling for Macklemore to be removed from the tour, arguing Sheeran's stage should not be used for "one-sided political propaganda".

Macklemore has rejected accusations that his comments were antisemitic.

By Monday, he was off the tour. Promoter Messina Touring Group said venue owners hosting upcoming dates had indicated they would not allow shows featuring Macklemore to proceed.

Sheeran's attempt to stay out of politics

The episode has highlighted the starkly different approaches the two artists take to their public platforms.

Macklemore has become increasingly outspoken about Gaza and has framed speaking about Palestinians from the stage as a moral obligation.

Sheeran, meanwhile, said this week that people attending his concerts "do not expect a political forum".

"I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes," he said.

"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace."

READ MORE Israeli minister calls for Oscar-winning film directors to be stripped of citizenship

Sheeran said he instead wants his shows to provide "safety and sanctuary" and bring together people from different backgrounds.

That doesn't mean Sheeran has always avoided political issues or humanitarian causes. In 2022, he performed at the televised Concert for Ukraine, which raised millions for people affected by Russia's invasion. He has also previously spoken publicly on issues including Brexit and LGBTQ+ equality.

But the singer has long resisted being characterised primarily as a political artist.

'I am not complicit'

Sheeran has also rejected suggestions he personally silenced Macklemore.

He said Macklemore had been allowed to choose his own setlist and that his contract for the tour was with the promoter.

Sheeran said he spent the week speaking with venues and was involved in discussions with promoters and activists on both sides in an effort to find a solution that would allow the tour to continue.

Ultimately, he said, the venues and promoter made the final decision.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," Sheeran said.

"I am not complicit."

Artists walk away from Sheeran's tour

The dispute has now spread beyond Macklemore, with several artists withdrawing from Sheeran's tour in solidarity.

According to Reuters, singer-songwriter Finneas, Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe have pulled out, while Irish band Beoga — which had been serving as Sheeran's touring band — is also leaving.

"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas said.

Rowe and Beoga both invoked Ireland's history in explaining their decisions.

Sheeran said he had spent the week trying to find a way forward that would allow Macklemore (pictured) to remain on the tour, including speaking directly with venues, promoters and activists on both sides of the issue. Credit: Invision

Beoga said its members were "Irish people who understand colonialism" and pointed to their involvement with the Irish Artists for Palestine movement.

Rowe, who described Sheeran as a friend who had changed his life, said he could not stand by while powerful people silenced those who spoke out.

Lukas Graham described its withdrawal as a "difficult decision", while arguing that wealth should not determine who was able to participate in public debate.

Why was Macklemore removed?

Macklemore has long publicly supported Palestinians and criticised Israel's military campaign in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.

In 2024, he released the protest song Hind's Hall in solidarity with pro-Palestinian demonstrators and in memory of five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab, who was killed in Gaza.

Macklemore has claimed New England Patriots NFL team owner Robert Kraft, whose Massachusetts stadium is hosting two upcoming Sheeran concerts, rallied stadium owners against his involvement in the tour.

READ MORE Australia sanctions Israeli extremists in response to violence in Palestine

Kraft has said he has dedicated significant time to fighting hate and antisemitism and felt a responsibility to intervene when he believed "that line has been crossed". Reuters reported Kraft had not publicly addressed Macklemore's specific claim that he rallied other stadium owners.

Pro-Israeli groups and US singer Pink, who is Jewish, have also criticised Macklemore, arguing comments made at concerts could compromise the safety of Jewish and pro-Israeli attendees.

Critics have also pointed to a 2014 appearance in which Macklemore wore a costume featuring a black wig, beard and fake hooked nose, which was criticised for invoking antisemitic stereotypes. Macklemore later apologised.

Macklemore has denied his recent comments were antisemitic, arguing that criticism of Israel's actions should not be conflated with antisemitism.

Sheeran's US tour is scheduled to resume in Philadelphia on 19 September.

title: From 'cashies' to convictions: The ATO's $2.7 million warning shot
text:
Key Points More than 350 individuals or businesses have been successfully prosecuted as part of a shadow economy crackdown.

The prosecutions related to tax avoidance and underpayment of entitlements.

Hundreds of people and businesses have been prosecuted for tax offences, with millions of dollars in fines handed down as authorities crack down on the shadow economy.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) on Thursday revealed non-lodgment prosecutions against "dodgy shadow economy operators" had risen by 80 per cent over the past two years, as it warned those who broke the rules would be held accountable.

The shadow economy involves both legal and illegal economic activity, including demanding cash payments for work, known as "cashies", to avoid tax, and underpayment of entitlements such as superannuation.

The ATO said more than 350 individuals or businesses had been successfully prosecuted in the past two years, resulting in more than $2.7 million in fines.

In the 2025-26 financial year, Queensland accounted for 28 per cent of non-lodgment prosecutions, followed by Western Australia (26 per cent) and NSW (20 per cent).

ATO assistant commissioner Tony Goding said avoiding tax and super obligations was seen by some as a victimless crime, but came at a cost to the community.

ATO assistant commissioner Tony Goding said those who were breaking the rules would be held to account. Source: Supplied / ATO

"The shadow economy undermines legitimate businesses and reduces revenue that would otherwise fund essential public services that support all Australians," he said.

"It doesn't matter what profession you're in, if you're a tradie, hairdresser or cafe owner, and you deliberately avoid paying the right amount of tax, you risk more than financial penalties."

Of the prosecutions, more than 305 resulted in convictions, representing a nearly 60 per cent increase from 2024–25 and 2025–26 financial years.

Goding said the figures demonstrated the ATO was holding those who break the rules to account.

"People who deliberately break the law risk their reputation and future, and the impact of a criminal conviction extends beyond the courtroom," he said.

"The cost of deliberately not lodging isn't measured in fines alone.

READ MORE A common tax misconception could catch some Australians by surprise

"We've seen business owners receive criminal convictions, lose the trust of their customers and community, and in some cases, lose the very business they were trying to keep afloat. For more serious offending, time in prison is even a possibility.

"Our message to the community is clear: deliberately ignoring your obligations comes at a significant cost."

A 2016 government task force estimated Australia's shadow economy could be worth as much as 3 per cent of GDP, or approximately $50 billion in 2016 figures.

More recent ATO estimates show the shadow economy has continued to grow, reaching up to 5.4 per cent of GDP in 2023.

title: Live updates: Major migration changes unveiled as Burke rejects Albanese speech claim
text:
Tougher sanctions for visa overstayers

Burke said the government will impose tougher sanctions on visa overstayers, returning to a scheme in place before 2015.

Before 2015, Burke said visa overstayers would be taken into detention, and within a few weeks, they'd organise their own flight and leave.

"That didn't just affect them. It had a behavioural impact," he said.

"The whole lot of other people who were overstaying thought, 'yeah, it's better that I just get on a plane and leave'."

He said that would not involve "the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries".

The government is also looking at alternative places for detention, including at a former quarantine facility in Melbourne.

He said there will be an additional 100 compliance officers and 250 beds.

"Effectively, what we are going back to doing is simply being able to make sure that if you overstay, you will not be able to say, 'Well, there's no consequences, as if they're ever going to make sure that I leave'," he said.

The code for migration agents will also be changed, with those who encourage claims without merit to be sanctioned and de-registered.

"It's something that should have happened some time ago, and we cannot have people with some sort of official formal status using that official formal status to encourage people to make something which, by any definition, is an unacceptable abuse of the system," Burke said.

He said the reforms were about making sure the system was "working as best as possible for the Australian economy".

— Miles Proust

title: US Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023, defying Trump
text:
In brief Experts anticipate at least one more rate hike by the US Federal Reserve by the end of this year.

The decision is likely to ease doubts that the Fed chief would hold off on tighter policy out of deference to Trump.

United States President Donald Trump has demanded interest rates be cut to 1 per cent after the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates on Thursday for the first time since 2023.

The Fed voted unanimously to raise rates by 0.25 percentage points, saying the rate hike would support a "timelier return" to its 2 per cent target for inflation.

It was a blow for Trump, who appointed central bank chief Kevin Warsh in the hopes that he would lower rates.

Instead, in his first major decision, the opposite was done.

Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social to speak out against the rise, saying rates should be less than 1 per cent and that the US could no longer "carry" other countries.
