But he stopped short of criticising Warsh personally.

"Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR," Trump wrote on Thursday morning.

United States Donald Trump took to social media to say interest rates needed to be lowered — "and fast". Source: Truth Social / Donald Trump

He said that if they stopped trading with countries with a deficit, the US would make "at least" US$1.5 trillion ($2.1 trillion) a year. He did not cite a source for that figure.

"We are "carrying" almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer," he added, before ending with: "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"

Trump-appointed Warsh defies pressure

It's ‌the first policy shift ‌under the new Fed chief, ⁠who took office in late May after being selected by Trump with an expectation that he would cut rates.

Warsh stressed the need to combat inflation that has been "too high" for "too long" and said the decision was a "serious" one, but needed to be taken.

"The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long," he told a press conference.

And the hike may not be the last — the vast majority of Fed policymakers indicated that at least one more rate hike was likely necessary before the end of the year, according to their Summary of Economic Projections.

US households and businesses have been battered by years of higher-than-target inflation, and prices have surged in the wake of Trump's war on Iran, his signature tariff policies and the ongoing AI boom.

Trump has launched an unprecedented assault on the Fed's independence since taking office, attempting to fire a Fed governor and launching a criminal probe against Warsh's predecessor in his quest for lower rates to spur economic activity.

Trump's Republican Party faces a stern test in the upcoming midterm elections, with rival Democrats seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress and with economic issues front and centre for voters.

White House calls rate hike decision 'unfortunate'

US stock markets largely priced in Thursday's rate hike, but they were still down on the news — expected with any rate hike as equities become less attractive.

Yields on 10-year US Treasury bonds — which have surged in recent days as uncertainty on long-term inflation has spiked — were also up past the 5 per cent threshold.

Following the Fed's announcement, White House spokesperson Kush Desai said the decision was "rather unfortunate" and that Trump had been clear that he wanted lower interest rates.

Warsh was named to his position after a contentious Senate confirmation process, where Democratic lawmakers accused him of being a "sock puppet" for Trump, which he denied.

So far, Trump has supported Warsh, claiming that the Fed chair wants lower rates and accusing the board of being "political."

The Fed has a dual mandate to deliver maximum employment while keeping inflation to its long-term 2 per cent target.

It mainly achieves these goals by setting the key US interest rate — lower rates tend to spur economic activity but fuel inflation, and hiking them cools both activity and prices.

title: 'Mobilisation of fear': The deeper strategy behind One Nation's immigration policy
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Jyoti has called her migration agent three times this month. Each time, she asks the same question: Has there been any update?

Her application for a Skilled Independent visa, a pathway to permanent residency, has been sitting in the queue for months. It has felt like a long wait for Jyoti, who has lived in Australia for the better part of a decade. In recent months, that uncertainty has taken on a new urgency.

The 43-year-old is a secondary school teacher who lives in an outer northern suburb of Melbourne with her husband and their two children. She arrived from Punjab, northern India, eight years ago as an international student and is now in Australia on a work visa.

She asks that only her first name be used because she fears speaking publicly could affect her family's visa prospects.

I feel like the axe is going to fall on people like us before anyone else.

"International students, temporary visa holders ... we would be the first to lose our livelihoods and our place here if Pauline Hanson comes to power, or if her party keeps gaining momentum," she tells SBS News.

Jyoti says she is watching the lead-up to Victoria's November election closely. To her, the election will be an early test of how far One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's momentum could travel and what that could mean for her family's future in the only country her children have really known. It's a fear, she says, that everyone she knows in her position is carrying right now.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

One Nation wants to cut 750,000 temporary visa holders from Australia over three years. Not one of them will get a say in whether the party succeeds.

"Our fate is being decided by political parties whose fate we have no say in," Jyoti says.

Australia is home to roughly three million temporary visa holders, including students, graduates and skilled workers.

As One Nation pushes for sweeping cuts to temporary migration, it raises a harder question about political power: are people with the least ability to influence an election also the easiest to target?

Who One Nation's visa cuts would hit hardest

One Nation's plan would tighten the student and graduate visa systems, restrict family members from accompanying temporary skilled workers, and close off "visa hopping" — the practice of extending a stay by switching between visa categories rather than leaving the country and reapplying offshore.

According to the policy announced on Monday, international students and graduates would absorb the biggest cuts.

The student visa population, including accompanying family members, would fall from about 590,000 to 350,000, and the graduate visa population from about 270,000 to just 40,000 over three years.

Family visas linked to temporary skilled workers would be phased out entirely, a change expected to shrink that cohort from about 263,000 to 160,000 over the same period.

Source: SBS News

"Tinkering around the edges will not fix the damage," Hanson said in the media release.

"This is about giving Australians breathing space by drastically cutting the stock of temporary migrants, restoring control and making sure migration serves Australia."

Speaking with ABC's Radio National on Monday morning, Environment Minister Murray Watt said One Nation's policy would trigger economic disruption.

"One Nation's policy is a recipe to destroy the Australian economy and drive the Australian economy into recession," he said.

For people already living that reality, the question isn't abstract. Jyoti says the proposed changes have made getting permanent residency feel less like the obvious next step in her journey and more like a race against time.

They are looking at us as just numbers, but there are actual lives and people behind these numbers.

Not everyone would be affected equally, says Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the Department of Immigration. Much depends on a migrant's professional skills and experience.

"Temporary entrants with skills in strong demand tend to secure permanent residency much faster than others," he tells SBS News.

Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the Department of Immigration, says One Nation's immigration policy would significantly affect Australia's education industry, which relies heavily on international students. Source: SBS News / Ewa Staszewska

For instance, a nurse's pathway to permanent residency looks nothing like that of a graduate in a field with weaker demand. For the latter, the road can be far longer, and far less certain.

One Nation has confirmed it would maintain a net overseas migration (NOM) ceiling of 130,000 a year once its proposed three-year reset is complete.

Rizvi says that target leaves the policy with nowhere else to land.

"Taking into account the fact that One Nation has said it wants to quarantine WHMs [Working Holiday Makers] and PALM [Pacific Australia Labour Mobility] visas from any cuts; cannot lawfully reduce places for partners and dependent children; can't easily reduce numbers of NZ citizens contributing to NOM and wants to maintain a flow of tradies and health workers, it leaves no room for students and temporary graduates," he says.

Essentially, One Nation policy would mean abolishing the international education industry.

"That would have massive consequences for university budgets and staff. Possibly 50,000 jobs would be directly affected. More indirectly."

The political cost of having no vote

Temporary entrants have never had voting rights in Australia and "never will", Rizvi says.

But it's a dynamic that has shaped migration policy for longer than many realise, says Emily Foley, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Canberra who studies social democratic and centre-left political parties.

She says temporary migration has quietly created problems over many decades that successive governments have had little reason to confront.

Emily Foley says temporary migration quietly created problems that governments had "minimal political incentive" to address. Source: Supplied

"For years, policymakers and governments knew there were significant issues with the temporary migration program essentially creating an underclass of exploited and marginalised workers," she tells SBS News.

"And yet, precisely because this cohort are not voters, there was minimal political incentive to actively discuss the policy area, particularly when migration was such a salient and politicised election issue."

One Nation is not alone in pushing for tighter controls on temporary migration. Labor has already moved to amend parts of its policy, including restricting visa hopping, shortening Temporary Graduate visas, raising the income threshold for temporary skilled migration and introducing managed limits on new international student commencements.

The Coalition has also promised to reduce migration by linking NOM to the number of homes built. It has separately proposed making compliance with an Australian Values Statement a universal visa condition, with breaches potentially leading to visa refusal or cancellation.

But One Nation's proposal goes considerably further, targeting the temporary migrant population with sharp reductions in student and graduate numbers and restrictions on accompanying family members.

Foley says the party's focus is consistent with its longstanding position on immigration.

Attacking temporary migrants is therefore not surprising.

"This cohort, despite many being Australian taxpayers, are without the civil, political and economic rights and privileges of Australian citizens and permanent residents. It is easy for parties like One Nation to attack and marginalise temporary migrants precisely because they have so little recourse."

Benjamin Moffitt, a senior lecturer in politics and international relations at Monash University, is more blunt about the electoral calculus.

"It removes the one thing that usually keeps rhetoric in check: the people it hits getting a vote on it," he tells SBS News.

"Temporary visa holders and prospective migrants can't punish a party at the ballot box, so there's no electoral cost to going as hard as you like on them.

"That's true of migration policy generally, not a One Nation quirk, but it's a big part of why this is the one area where the inflammatory rhetoric can run so far ahead of the actual policy detail."

Benjamin Moffitt says political parties understand that temporary visa holders and prospective migrants have no direct electoral leverage because they cannot vote. Source: Supplied / Nish Paranavitana

But he stops short of saying One Nation is deliberately targeting temporary migrants for this reason.

What can be established, Moffitt says, is that the groups One Nation has identified most precisely — including international students, working holidaymakers and skilled visa holders — are among those who cannot vote.

"Whether that's a deliberate strategy of picking targets who can't retaliate, or simply where the populist radical right's usual scapegoating logic lands by default, isn't something you can necessarily tell apart from the outside."

One Nation did not respond to SBS News' request for comment on whether the lack of voting rights among temporary visa holders is a consideration in its immigration policies.

What temporary migrants contribute

Temporary migrants make up a significant part of Australia's workforce and international education sector. Their contribution extends beyond the visa system , with international students alone generating almost $55 billion in education export income in 2025.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, international students and their families accounted for 82.4 per cent of non-residents eligible to work in Australia in June 2025.

Andrew McKellar, CEO of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told reporters on Monday that cutting temporary migration to the degree proposed by One Nation could have a significant economic impact.

"You know, if you're going to cut overall visa levels by 750,000 over a three-year period and drive net overseas migration into negative territory, that's a COVID-level shock to the Australian economy," he said.

One Nation has pointed to Canada's recent cuts to temporary migration as evidence that immigration can be reduced without crashing the economy.

McKellar said the focus should instead be on the potential impact of the proposed cuts on Australia's growth.

"What the debate cannot be about is it cannot be about arbitrary targets. We can't have solutions which are extreme, which would cause very significant damage to the Australian economy."

Why immigration works for One Nation

Tiziana Torresi is the program director of the School of Society and Culture at Adelaide University and studies normative political theory and the governance of migration. She says immigration sits within a broader populist strategy that divides society between an "authentic" Australian public and groups portrayed as threatening to its interests.

"Anti-immigration rhetoric has been central to One Nation's political discourse from its emergence," she tells SBS News.

Tiziana Torresi says the One Nation's appeal taps into Australian voters' economic and social anxieties. Source: Supplied

Torresi says the party's appeal taps into economic and social anxieties.

"The mobilisation of fear is a key strategy of populist far-right parties, enabling them to present themselves as the only true voice and defenders of an authentic national community threatened by 'outsiders'," she says.

Moffitt says this extends to issues such as housing, jobs and infrastructure. He describes this approach as 'nativism', where social and economic problems are attributed to outsiders, particularly migrants.

"Nativism doesn't identify a housing crisis and then, separately, decide migrants are to blame; it needs a scapegoat for social and economic ills, and the migrant is the figure built to supply one," he says.

The result is a message that can speak to voters worried about the cost of living, housing and population growth, while also tapping into deeper concerns about Australia's changing social and cultural identity.

Torresi says this allows One Nation to present itself as the party willing to restore a sense of control to voters who believe established political parties have failed them.

One Nation can exploit these various anxieties by claiming that 'ordinary Australians' are being left behind or displaced.

That is where the politics of temporary migration becomes more complicated. The people most directly affected may have no vote, but the issue is being used to speak to millions of people who do.

Beyond the ballot box

Torresi says the absence of a vote does not mean migrants are politically disconnected.

"Migrants are embedded in families, workplaces, neighbourhoods, unions, community organisations, and broader social networks, creating relationships with citizens who do possess electoral rights," she says.

Those relationships can give migrants an indirect political voice through the citizens around them, who can respond at the ballot box.

"Consequently, political attacks on migrants may have effects that extend well beyond the migrant population itself."

But temporary migrants may have fewer connections to Australian citizens who can advocate for their interests, Torresi says.

"Temporary migrants may be doubly vulnerable to anti-immigration politics because they can lack both direct and indirect forms of political influence."

Back in Melbourne, Jyoti says the fear she feels is being mirrored back to her.

"It's not just me. Everyone I know in this situation feels the same fear," she says.

We've built our lives here, and none of that means we get a say in what happens to us next.

Her migration agent still doesn't have an update. She'll call again next week.

title: An ancient disease is surging in Australia — and it isn't always easy to detect
text:
IN BRIEF Gonorrhoea and syphilis notifications have surged by more than half in the past decade.

Indigenous health experts have warned of a serious need for investment in community-led health projects.

Reported cases of infectious syphilis and gonorrhoea have surged by more than half over the past decade in Australia, as experts warn education and testing urgently needs to improve.

In 2025, there were 42,393 gonorrhoea notifications and 5,986 infectious syphilis notifications — a 10-year increase of 57 per cent for gonorrhoea and 56 per cent for syphilis, analysis from the University of New South Wales' Kirby Institute has shown.

Syphilis was declared a communicable disease of national significance in late 2025, in response to "ongoing and concerning" rises in Australian case numbers.

Chief medical officer Professor Michael Kidd declared that awareness was necessary among all Australians, including healthcare professionals, and urged everyone to get tested.

Syphilis and gonorrhoea are common bacterial infections with ancient origins, now easily treated with antibiotics.

But both infections can present with either mild or non-existent symptoms.

If left untreated, syphilis progresses through stages and can spread to the brain, heart, eyes, and other organs. It can cause neurological problems including paralysis, and dementia, and cause soft, tumour-like growths to appear on the skin, bones or internal organs. Tertiary syphilis can eventually lead to death.

Chlamydia remained the most frequently diagnosed STI in 2025, followed by gonorrhoea, then syphilis. Source: SBS News / The Kirby Institute

Notification rates for infectious syphilis among women increased 170 per cent in the past decade from 2016 to 2025. In contrast, rates increased just 39 per cent among males.

Syphilis during pregnancy can lead to congenital syphilis, which can result in miscarriage or stillbirth, or severe lifelong health impacts in babies that are born, including prematurity, low birthweight and other physical developmental abnormalities.

Kirby Institute epidemiologist Dr Skye McGregor said congenital syphilis is a persistent issue in Australia, with more than half of deaths in the last decade among First Nations infants. There were 14 cases of congenital syphilis in 2025, and 113 from 2016 to 2025, with 40 resulting in the death of an infant.

"This is an entirely preventable outcome with early diagnosis, testing and treatment of pregnant people," McGregor said.

Better approaches for at-risk populations

First Nations peoples were disproportionately affected by STIs, diagnosed with gonorrhoea at more than four times the rate of non-Indigenous people and syphilis at more than six times.

Kim Gates, community relations lead in the Kirby Institute's First Nations Point-Of-Care Program, said the disparities in diagnoses between First Nations and non-Indigenous Australians were an indication of broader inequities in healthcare.

READ MORE Stolen Generations survivors face worse health outcomes than other First Nations people

Australian services needed to be designed better to reflect the experiences of First Nations communities, Gates told SBS News, adding that many First Nations peoples have a complex relationship with the Australian health system and "have good reasons to be sceptical of top-down services and approaches".

"This is why Aboriginal-led services are so important," she said.

Gates said that while the 149 Aboriginal Controlled Community Health Services in Australia provide comprehensive and culturally safe healthcare, "there are areas these don't reach".

READ MORE This Australian crisis is entering a 'confronting' new phase

For Gates, sustained investment in community-led initiatives, like the First Nations Molecular Point-of-Care Testing Program, was the solution to bringing down STI rates among Indigenous populations.

Improving community awareness is key

Dr Arthur Wong, sexual health physician and conjoint lecturer at the Kirby Institute, said that timely testing, treatment and retesting were "crucial", and that post-diagnosis care was also "essential" to avoid repeat infections.

Wong told SBS News that awareness was already affecting syphilis rates, where evidence shows a decline in incidence among gay and bisexual men.

"We do know that testing has increased in certain populations," Wong said. "Gay and bisexual men who are taking HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PReP) are tested more frequently for STIs."

But the data leaves out an often-overlooked section of the population — for homosexual, bisexual and transgender women, rates of syphilis and gonorrhoea remain largely unknown.

LGBTIQ+ Women's Project Lead at ACON (formerly AIDS Council of NSW), Lee Wang, says queer and trans women aren't routinely reported in surveillance data, which has adverse health outcomes.

"When queer and trans women are overlooked, it can create the false impression that STI prevention and testing are not relevant to them," Wang told SBS News.

"This can contribute to lower testing and missed opportunities for prevention and early diagnosis, with recent surveys highlighting substantial gaps in STI testing when compared with gay and bisexual men."

There was a need for targeted sexual health education resources, Wang said, like ACON's Word on the Sheets, a digital sexual and reproductive health resource for LGBTQ+ women, trans and gender diverse people.

"We shouldn't confuse a lack of data with a lack of priority," Wang said. "We need healthcare providers who are equipped to discuss sexual practices without making assumptions about sexuality or gender identity."

Wong said preliminary data from the most recent Australian Study of Health and Relationships show that just 17 per cent of people aged 16 to 49 reported having an STI test in the last 12 months.

Rates of chlamydia and gonorrhoea were highest among young people aged 15 to 29 years.

Studies in recent years have pointed to a waning use of condoms among school-aged people in Australia, with findings from a Secondary Students and Sexual Health (SSASH) survey analysis by Victoria University in 2024 stating that condom use in Australia was low and has declined over a decade.

Overall, Wong said, Australia needed a "sustained and enhanced" response to sexual health, "to ensure any gains are experienced equally across all populations."

title: EU proposes landmark associate membership for Canada
text:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union is opening the door for Canada to become its first "associate member", a status that is not set out in the bloc's treaties.

Von der Leyen's announcement is a significant shift in EU policy. The bloc has historically resisted flexible categories and EU members were lukewarm in reacting to Germany's proposal in May of associate membership for Ukraine as a stepping stone to full accession.

"Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system," von der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

"We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics. And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all ... Europe and Canada believe in democracy."

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this week Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU but not membership. Von der Leyen invited Carney to join her in Strasbourg, and he will make his own address on Thursday.

title: 'Really problematic': Australians are rejecting the very homes the country needs
text:
IN BRIEF New home sales fell 10 per cent in August and are now at their lowest level in more than a year.

Experts say high borrowing and construction costs are making the new homes Australia needs harder to afford.

Buyers appear to be rejecting newly-built homes, sparking concerns Australia's property market slowdown could worsen a chronic housing shortage.

Sales of new homes fell 10 per cent nationally in August and were 19.3 per cent lower in the three months to August compared with the previous quarter, according to new data from the Housing Industry Association (HIA).

Sales have now fallen for four consecutive months to their lowest level in more than a year.

The slowdown was recorded across all five mainland states included in the HIA survey, which tracks sales by large-volume home builders and is considered a leading indicator of future detached home construction.

Victoria recorded the sharpest quarterly decline, with sales down 27 per cent, followed by Queensland at 20.2 per cent, NSW at 17.5 per cent, South Australia at 10.8 per cent and Western Australia at 8.2 per cent.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

HIA chief economist Tim Reardon said the deterioration meant the recovery in new home building seen earlier this year had been interrupted.

"Today's new home sales are tomorrow's housing commencements," he said in a statement.

"The decline in sales through the middle of 2026 will mean fewer homes commencing construction in 2027."

Why are Australians pulling back?

Independent property economist Cameron Kusher told SBS News that a combination of higher borrowing costs and low confidence was making it increasingly difficult to buy a new home. But he warned that if sales continued to decline leading to fewer builds, it could lead to even higher prices in the future.

"We're seeing really weak confidence around the housing market generally at the moment," he told SBS News.

Tim Lawless, the research director at property data firm Cotality, said the slowdown was also evident across the broader property market, although new homes appeared to have been hit harder.

Cotality estimates home sales across the broader market were about 15 per cent lower over winter than a year earlier and 11 per cent below the five-year average.

"It does look like new home sales have been hit a little bit harder," Lawless said, pointing to higher interest rates, weaker confidence, reduced investment and affordability and serviceability constraints.

The slowdown has been particularly pronounced in Sydney, Brisbane and Perth, where Cotality estimates home sales fell by more than 20 per cent over winter compared with the same period last year.

Lawless said Brisbane and Perth were coming off relatively strong levels of activity, while Sydney's decline was more reflective of severe affordability constraints.

Kusher said new homes typically carried a premium compared with established properties, making older homes more desirable as household borrowing capacity comes under pressure.

"Buyers are asking themselves: "Am I prepared to pay the premium for a brand-new home when I can get an older home, an established home, cheaper?"

"I'm not surprised that we're seeing these ongoing falls, but obviously that's really problematic when you need to be building more homes."

The HIA data does not provide a detailed breakdown of the types or price points of detached homes experiencing the greatest decline.

But Kusher said affordability was clearly becoming a bigger constraint.

Higher interest rates mean some prospective buyers simply aren't able to borrow enough to buy the homes they otherwise might have considered.

HIA has also pointed to rising construction costs, taxation and broader economic uncertainty as factors weighing on the sector.

Reardon said builders were reporting fewer people visiting display sites, declining enquiries and preliminary commitments, and rising cancellation rates.

Lawless agreed, telling SBS News that higher material, labour and other construction costs were also making new homes less competitive with established properties.

Why today's sales matter for tomorrow's housing supply

Government figures show there were 244,000 dwellings under construction in the March quarter of 2026, the most since records began in 1984.

The deterioration in sales is unlikely to immediately show up in housing commencements this year.

The problem comes further down the pipeline, with the impact of weaker sales expected to become more apparent in 2027.

Lawless said some projects may have become financially unviable as construction and labour costs increased, while others may not have secured enough pre-sales to trigger financing.

"Typically most developers would need to have a minimum level of pre-sales before a lender is going to be becoming active in the credit supply," he said.

Kusher said most builders sought to secure a buyer before starting construction rather than building homes speculatively and hoping to sell them afterwards.

Financing speculative construction was particularly difficult when both borrowing and construction costs were high, he said.

That means the relationship between weaker sales and fewer future homes is relatively straightforward.

"If people aren't buying homes, you're not likely to get many homes built," Kusher said.

In 2024 the National Housing Accord commenced with an aspirational target of 1.2 million new, well-located homes over the five years to June 2029.

The target was agreed between federal, state and territory governments, local government and industry in an effort to substantially increase housing supply.

Government figures show this is already behind targets and likely won't be met until the end of 2030, and Kusher warns it could get blown out further still.

Australia needs homes — but at what price?

The slowdown creates a difficult contradiction for Australia's housing market.

Demand has not disappeared simply because fewer people can afford to buy a newly built home.

"The thing with the shortage of supply in housing is that price matters," Kusher said.

"We need more houses, but they need to be at a price that people can afford."

Lawless described the construction sector as being caught "between a rock and a hard place".

"A builder or a developer, obviously, they're not going to be building homes if there's no profit to be had, and consumers or households aren't going to be buying new homes if they're too expensive to purchase," he said.

HIA similarly warned the decline in new home sales was occurring without an equivalent decline in Australia's underlying need for housing, pointing to population growth, low unemployment and the existing shortage of homes.

What could turn the market around?

HIA has warned that further interest rate rises would place additional pressure on a new home market already struggling with weaker demand.

"This is not the time for another rate rise," Reardon said.

Kusher, however, said getting inflation under control was ultimately necessary to restore stability to the housing market — even if doing so meant households faced more financial pressure in the short term.

He said longer-term improvement depended on bringing inflation under control, allowing greater certainty to return to the economy and eventually creating scope for borrowing costs to fall.

"Now that means higher interest rates, and that means it's going to be hard for people."

But he said easing inflation could ultimately provide the conditions needed for both property prices and borrowing costs to stabilise, "and that's when you'll start to see things improve."

title: Nyadol Nyuon responds to criticism over 'no white culture' remarks
text:
IN BRIEF The lawyer says race and culture should not be conflated, arguing there is no single "white culture".

Nyuon previously began returning her OAM as part of what she called her "slow and certain" departure from Australia.

Lawyer and human rights advocate Nyadol Nyuon has defended her claim that there is "no white culture" after remarks she made turning a televised debate drew criticism.

Nyuon appeared on the ABC's National Forum on migration on Monday, where she rejected the idea Australia was historically monocultural and said she had "no intention of assimilating".

But she stressed that did not mean rejecting Australia, its laws or the country she says she "deeply" loves.

She argued that describing Australia as an "Anglo-Celtic culture" risked creating the impression there was a single "white culture" migrants were expected to adopt.

"There is Italian culture, there is French culture, there is Argentinian culture, but there is not this notion of sort of a white culture that is being threatened," Nyuon told the forum.

The discussion came amid a broader national debate about migration, multiculturalism and what it means to be Australian.

Following criticism of her remarks, Nyuon expanded on the argument in a social media post on her LinkedIn account.

'No white culture'

"Apparently, saying there is no white culture has offended some people," she wrote on Tuesday.

"There is no white culture as there is no black culture."

Nyuon argued that race and culture should not be treated as interchangeable, pointing to the cultural differences that exist between people who may otherwise be grouped together according to skin colour.

"Black is a colour, not a culture. There are Black people. There is Ethiopian culture," she wrote.

Nyuon also defended her argument that Australia had never been monocultural, pointing to the hundreds of First Nations that existed before colonisation as well as the long histories of Chinese migrants and Afghan cameleers in Australia.

A debate over belonging

During the forum, former deputy prime minister John Anderson argued there were legitimate concerns among Australians about social cohesion and whether some groups respected Australian culture and values.

Anderson described those values as including individual dignity, equality before the law and the separation of the secular and sacred.

Nyuon acknowledged Australians had a right to be concerned about threats to social cohesion but challenged the way the issue was being framed.

She argued the migration debate could become a proxy for conversations about race and questioned why a person's appearance should influence perceptions of their belonging.

"Whenever we attempt to speak about how our belonging can look like, you meet such resistance, and the majority of the time that resistance comes from how you look," she said on Monday.

'I love this country'

Nyuon also spoke about her complicated relationship with Australia and her previously announced intention to begin the process of renouncing her Australian citizenship.

The lawyer, who was born in a refugee camp in Ethiopia after her family fled the Sudanese civil war, came to Australia as a teenager.

In April, Nyuon revealed she had written to the governor-general's office to begin returning the Medal of the Order of Australia she was awarded in 2022 for "service to human rights and refugee women".

"This is the first step in my slow and certain process of leaving Australia and releasing my connections to this country," she wrote at the time.

Nyuon said she remained "so grateful" to Australia and would "always be indebted to it", but linked her decision to her experiences with Victoria University and WorkSafe Victoria.

Nyuon resigned from Victoria University in 2025, after overseeing an $800,000 WorkSafe Victoria project aimed at preventing workplace gendered violence, which was plagued by delays, strained relationships and resourcing issues.

An independent evaluator later found instability and mismanagement meant it could not properly assess the program's success.

Speaking on National Forum, she said she loved Australia but was conscious that political circumstances could affect whether she and her children felt they could remain.

"Many migrants deeply, deeply love this country. I love this country," she said.

In her subsequent LinkedIn post, Nyuon maintained her comments about culture were not intended as an insult.

title: Tony Burke set to unveil Labor's new migration plan amid working holiday visa concerns
text:

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has repeatedly declined to provide further details, refusing to set a timeframe for migration announcements and saying they would be made at "appropriate times".

What could Labor be planning?

Labor has previously proposed reducing net overseas migration and set an annual target of 225,000 by 2027-28.

Burke has already flagged plans to make more changes to the visa system to curb net overseas migration, with the government officially confirming in August that it would slow the processing of working holiday visa applications.

The horticulture and tourism sectors have been calling for certainty, raising fears that a backlog of working holiday visas could mean there aren't enough workers for regional businesses in the summer months.

Labor is also expected to tighten rules for international students and their families and further restrict some visitor visas.

Potential changes could prevent international students from switching courses to extend their stay, increase scrutiny of onshore visa applications, limit the number of family members attached to student visas, and restrict transfers from higher education into vocational education and training programs.

Some tourist visas are also expected to be reduced from 12 months to six months.

The Albanese government has already confirmed that Australia's annual humanitarian intake of 20,000 places will not be reduced.

Burke has previously argued migration plans should be considered alongside housing supply, saying in June: "If you go at migration the wrong way, then you can actually make the housing situation worse."

Political pressure builds

Negotiations between the government and the Coalition over migration settings have stalled over the last week, with the Opposition pushing for deeper cuts to net overseas migration and stronger powers around deportation.

But both parties have criticised One Nation's plan revealed on Monday saying it would "shock" the economy and devastate the construction, health and aged care sectors.

One Nation proposed cutting temporary migration by more than 750,000 places over three years, arguing Australia's migration system requires a major "reset".

Under the policy, international students, recent graduates and their family members would be hit hardest, with migration places in those categories reduced by almost 470,000 over three years.

Burke has told SBS News he tried to find a path for bipartisan agreement with the Opposition.

"I had hoped that the Opposition would work constructively to make sure the immigration minister of the day had additional powers to be able to regulate net overseas migration," he said on Wednesday.

"At the moment, they haven't agreed to measures which they claim to support.

"I would much rather have more targeted levers available."

Independent ACT senator David Pocock took aim at Labor on Wednesday morning, saying current conversations about migration were "unproductive" and had to factor in what the country needed over the next 10 years.

"The big thing I would love to see is a plan," he told ABC's Radio National.

"There's this constant talk about numbers, about classes of visas, rather than actually having the conversation as a country — what is our 10-year plan for migration?"

It was those "hard conversations" that were paramount to Australia's migration debate, he argued.

"To me, that’s how you solve this issue ... rather than having this ridiculous fight over a number that raises all sorts of concerns for aged care, for healthcare, for farmers who are relying on backpackers."

"It just seems so unproductive."

The Coalition is yet to release its migration policy, but has hinted that its plan will tie migration figures to the amount of new homes built, which is currently tracking around 173,000 per year.

Opposition defence spokesperson James Paterson said he was looking forward to seeing the detail of Labor's plan but was "deeply sceptical about Labor's ability to deliver, because for four years they've failed to deliver".

"As for our own policy, we are close to releasing it, but we're actually going to do the work to get it right because we are not the government," he told reporters in Canberra.

"We are seeking to be the government after the next election and we're not going to put out a half-baked policy like One Nation has that hasn't even been costed, the budgetary impacts of which they have no idea."

title: Four more acts quit Ed Sheeran tour as singer says Macklemore decision 'was not mine'
text:
IN BRIEF US rapper Macklemore said he was dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour this week after making pro-Palestinian comments.

He said on Monday that several US venues had vowed to prohibit him from appearing as Sheeran's opening act.

Four supporting acts have quit Ed Sheeran's tour after the rapper Macklemore was removed for pro-Palestinian comments he made during a concert in New Jersey.

Hours after Sheeran posted on social media about Macklemore's removal and attributed the decision to the tour's promoters, Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, the Danish band Lukas Graham, and Finneas posted on Instagram that they would withdraw from Sheeran's tour.

Rowe was one of Macklemore's replacements for Sheeran's remaining US dates, while Beoga was serving as Sheeran's touring band. Finneas, who is Billie Eilish's brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year.

Rowe and Beoga each cited their country's history in their statements explaining their decision.

"We are Irish people who understand colonialism. As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be," Beoga said.

"But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation," he said, saying he could not "stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up".

Finneas, who has publicly advocated for Palestinians in the past, reiterated his support.

"Money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody's bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we're allowed to acknowledge," the band posted, seemingly referring to billionaire Robert Kraft's role in Macklemore's removal from the tour.

Dropping Macklemore was 'promoter's decision', Sheeran says

Sheeran weighed in on Macklemore being dropped as his opening act after the rapper made pro-Palestinian comments onstage during their tour, saying the decision was made by the promoters alone. The British singer also said he refused to be drawn into a public discussion about the war in Gaza.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," Sheeran wrote on Instagram on Tuesday. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

Sheeran's statement came a day after Macklemore said he was kicked off the Loop Tour after exclaiming "Free Palestine!" during the 5 September date at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium while introducing his protest song Hind's Hall.

"To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you," he said during the concert.

Macklemore said on Monday on Instagram that several US venues told the promoter they would prohibit him from performing as Sheeran's opening act, rallied by Kraft, owner of the NFL's New England Patriots. His Kraft Group also owns Gillette Stadium, where the Patriots play.

title: Profits in Australia's property market still 'exceptionally high' despite recent downturn
text:
IN BRIEF New data from Cotality shows that 95.4 per cent of dwelling sales made a gain in the June quarter.

While dwelling values declined over the quarter, prices remained significantly higher than six years earlier.

Australia is undergoing one of the steepest housing downturns in decades, but years of strong growth mean most homes are still being sold for a hefty profit.

In the June quarter, 95.4 per cent of dwelling sales made a gain, down from the 21-year high of 96.1 per cent recorded in the three months to March, research from data provider Cotality showed on Wednesday.

While national dwelling values declined 1.5 per cent over the June quarter, prices were still more than 67 per cent higher than six years earlier.

Several years of very strong growth had left many home owners with a substantial equity buffer, helping vendors rake in a combined $35.9 billion in profit in the quarter, Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said.

"Profitability is still exceptionally high by historical standards, but we are starting to see the impact of weaker housing market conditions flow through to resale outcomes," Burg said.

"Most sellers are still benefiting from the significant value growth accumulated over the past five years, which is providing considerable protection against the early stages of the downturn.

"With home values falling across more markets, that buffer will become increasingly important in determining resale outcomes."

Australia's housing downturn continued to deepen in July and August, as the outlook for interest rates worsened and investors continued to count the cost of the federal government's changes to negative gearing and the capital gains discount.

READ MORE Why Australia's richest suburbs could be a warning for every homeowner

Nationwide prices are only down 3.6 per cent from their March peak, but several economists, including at HSBC and Morgan Stanley, expect the total fall in values to hit 10 per cent or more, which would be the deepest downturn in more than 40 years.

The pace of the decline has also rattled sentiment, with the 2022/23 downturn the only time prices have fallen faster for longer since the 1980s.

Buyers who held onto their property for a longer period of time were better able to ride out the cyclical ebbs and flows.

"Owners who have held their property for nine or 10 years have generally experienced several periods of value growth, giving them a much larger equity buffer when market conditions weaken," Burg said.

Houses that sold for a profit were held for a median 9.3 years, compared with the typical holding time of 4.4 years for loss-making house resales.

Overall, 97.8 per cent of houses were sold for a profit, underscoring the growth advantage of freestanding homes over units. Only 90.5 per cent of unit sales made a profit.

Sydney was still the top money spinner in dollar terms, with a total profit of $6.6 billion.

But the proportion of sales that made a profit eased to 92.7 per cent, well below Brisbane, which recorded a profit in 99.8 per cent of sales.

Nationally, the median gain eased from a record $378,000 to $371,000, while the median loss increased from $44,000 to $45,000.

title: Want a comfortable retirement? Here's the new super figure Australians need
text:
IN BRIEF Goods and services that retirees spend most on rise faster than inflation, a peak body says.

A comfortable retirement is becoming more expensive as a result.

Australians now need a little bit more in their super to retire comfortably, with the rising cost of living driving up the latest retirement standard.

A couple who own their home and are seeking a comfortable retirement will need $78,998 a year, or $1,513 a week. A single homeowner will need $56,166 a year, or $1,076 a week.

Those figures were released on Tuesday by the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA), the peak body for the super industry.

It showed for homeowners aged 65 to 84, the budget for a comfortable retirement rose 0.5 per cent for couples and 0.4 per cent for singles in the June quarter.

For a modest retirement, their budget rose 0.4 per cent for couples and 0.3 per cent for singles, to $52,690 and $36,548 a year respectively.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

For retirees aged 85 and over, a comfortable retirement will cost $74,484 per year for couples and $53,964 per year for singles. For retirees who rent privately, a modest budget is now $69,376 per year for a couple and $51,418 per year for a single.

ASFA CEO Mary Delahunty says retirees are being affected by the soaring cost of living more than others because the things they buy are rising quicker than the inflation rate of 3.8 per cent.

These include electricity, which the group said rose 22.4 per cent after federal and state rebates ended (22 per cent), car costs (6.5 per cent), medical services (5 per cent), insurance (almost 5 per cent) and meals out (4 per cent).

Source: SBS News

"Retirees are among the groups hit hardest by the cost of living crisis because their budgets are weighted towards the things going up in price the most," Delahunty said.

What's a comfortable retirement compared to a modest one?

AFSA defines a comfortable retirement as being able to afford quality private health insurance, eat out most weeks, and go on a yearly holiday in Australia or overseas every few years.

A modest retirement includes basic health cover, such as a hospital-only plan, domestic-only holidays, and occasional eating out.

On the age pension alone, it's a much slimmer budget with limited lifestyle and basic living spending.

"Most of these things drop out of your budget entirely," ASFA CEO Mary Delahunty said.

She said while the age pension goes up with inflation, it doesn't allow for spending on other things like private health and holidays, which are increasing in price, and leaving retirees more reliant on their super to make those payments.

"Super is the difference between watching every dollar and having a sense of financial security in retirement," Delahunty said.

READ MORE How much super do Australians need to retire? It could be less than you think

Superannuation as an election issue

As Australia nears a federal election, superannuation has become a major political campaign line as the parties try to win voters amid a cost of living crisis.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers signalled super could become a political issue at the next federal election, and accused his political opponents of trying to "end compulsory superannuation as we know it".

His calls came after Liberal senator Andrew Bragg declared superannuation an "illiberal experiment".

One Nation has proposed allowing workers paying rent or a mortgage to divert 3 per cent of their super payments straight to their wallet for up to three years — investing only 9 per cent instead of the current compulsory rate of 12 per cent.

READ MORE Labor reveals super increase position amid 'predatory' practices crackdown

The policy has come under criticism from super firms and the government, with some estimates that people opting into the scheme could lose $25,000 from their retirement fund.

ASFA calculates a similar loss, saying a 30-year-old on average full-time earnings who takes three years of super as cash under the One Nation proposal would receive around $54 a week now and retire with $23,900 less in today's dollars.

"The cost of living and housing crises need their own solutions. Forcing Australians to solve them by robbing from their own future selves is not a helping hand. It is a worse deal than previous generations had," Delahunty said.

title: Could a Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish independence pact threaten UK unity?
text:
In brief The Scottish National Party, Wales' Plaid Cymru and the pro-Irish unity Sinn Féin want to break away from the UK.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously rejected Northern Ireland or Scotland holding referendums on the matter.

Leaders of the main Scottish, Northern Irish and Welsh nationalist parties declared at a meeting overnight that they have the right to choose whether to stay in the United Kingdom, with all three seeing their future as nations within the European Union.

The Scottish National Party (SNP), Plaid Cymru in Wales, and the pro-Irish-unity Sinn Féin want to break away from the UK, although under different timelines and conditions.

The rare meeting in the Welsh capital came just days after United States President Donald Trump waded in on the issue, saying he would back a united Ireland.

His comments showed "the unity debate is very much alive", Northern Ireland's Michelle O'Neill said alongside fellow party leaders as they announced a memorandum of understanding.

"Our nations have the right to self-determination. No Westminster government (the UK government) has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future," the agreement said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

SNP leader John Swinney, Rhun ap Iorwerth, leader of Plaid Cymru in Wales, and Mary Lou McDonald and O'Neill, leader and deputy leader of Sinn Féin, met in their roles as party leaders, rather than as top officials in their respective governments.

O'Neill is Northern Ireland's first minister while Iorwerth and Swinney lead their respective nationalist parties in Scotland and Wales.

Where do Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland stand on the independence issue?

The agreement said that, for the first time, each nation had a first minister "committed to independence from the UK", adding: "The future of our nations belongs in the European Union."

The independence parties are the biggest in both the Scottish and Welsh parliaments for the first time since devolution measures began in 1999. Sinn Féin has been the biggest party in Northern Ireland's assembly since 2022.

The SNP wants a second independence referendum after an earlier ballot in 2014 saw Scotland narrowly vote to remain in Britain. Successive UK governments have ruled out an immediate rerun.

Sinn Féin, the former political wing of the paramilitary Irish Republican Army (IRA), wants a vote on the UK territory of Northern Ireland being reunified with Ireland.

Plaid Cymru seeks Welsh independence in the longer term, but Iorwerth has ruled out pressing for a referendum immediately.

Could an independence move succeed?

Laura McAllister, a politics professor at Cardiff University, said the deliberately broad term "self-determination" was used due to these differing timelines and goals.

"Plaid Cymru was elected with heavy emphasis on avoiding the issue of independence this term," she told Agence France-Presse (AFP).

Shortly after taking power, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Irish unity was "off the table".

The 1998 Good Friday peace agreement that largely ended three decades of conflict in Northern Ireland provides for a referendum if Westminster's Northern Ireland minister believes a majority is likely to favour joining the Republic of Ireland.

Sinn Féin leader McDonald said the prime minister had no authority to deny any provisions of the agreement, and Burnham backtracked in parliament last week.

On Monday, a spokesperson insisted that Burnham believed "strongly in the Union", the constitutional tie that makes Northern Ireland part of the UK.

On Scotland, Burnham told lawmakers there could be another vote if there was a "clear consensus" but later reportedly said a referendum remained "off limits".

"It is unlikely that this (meeting) will change the UK Government's refusal to allow a referendum in Scotland or, at present, Northern Ireland," said Michael Keating, an emeritus politics professor at the University of Aberdeen.

But the meeting was "significant politically", he told AFP, because the other parties long avoided association with Sinn Féin due to its link to the IRA.

Alex Kane, a former communications chief for Ireland's Ulster Unionist Party, pointed to the absence of Northern Ireland's deputy first minister, Emma Little-Pengelly, of the pro-UK Democratic Unionist Party.

Her post is of equal weight to O'Neill's under Belfast's power-sharing government and "neither can claim to represent the government of Northern Ireland if the other hasn't agreed to it," he told AFP.

Little-Pengelly slammed O'Neill, claiming her position was "weaponised" at "a summit of separatists".

The meeting sparked mixed reactions in Belfast.

"Ireland would be better off if it was one country and we were back in the EU," retiree Ray Dennison, 61, told AFP.

But Jim Boyle, a 64-year-old environmental worker, said the meeting filled him with "trepidation".

"Many years ago I may have wished for the break-up of the United Kingdom, now ... I just don't want anything that's unpredictable."

In a word: funky. Think boulder-shaped pink seats in the lobby and a dazzling spherical gold artwork by the lifts. Even the corridors have personality, with dark blue walls, black-and-white barcode-style carpet and distorting psychedelic mirrors. Things calm down in Sienna, the property’s ground-floor all-day eatery and lounge, where a relaxing palette of light woods and speckled stonework is softened by pot plants suspended from an exposed industrial ceiling. Bright blue accents are carried into the Tribe Extra City View bathroom. There are five room categories, ranging from windowless, 15-square-metre Tribe Essentials to spacious 25-square-metre suites with “city views” (aka the surrounding office blocks). All feature the same vibrant decor – bright blue walls, abstract prints and red, white and grey geometric carpet – along with compact tiled en suites with rain showers and refillable Kevin Murphy amenities. Tribe’s guiding ethos is “everything you need and nothing you don’t”, so while you can expect a comfortable queen bed, Nespresso machine, bar fridge and smart TV, you won’t find a bathrobe, mini-bar or pillow menu. There are a few space-saving compromises, such as wall-mounted hangers instead of a wardrobe and a handheld steamer rather than an ironing board, but overall the focus is on premium practicality. It’s a light, airy venue that works better during the day, when large sliding doors let in the buzz of the CBD. It has a much more appealing energy now, with after-work activity helping to revitalise the nightlife. From the hotel, you’re not far from Queen Street’s big-brand stores, Britomart’s independent boutiques and the buzzy Aotea Square, which often hosts markets, festivals and outdoor performances. Viaduct Harbour and Wynyard Quarter are a 15-minute stroll away, and it’s easy to forget how lovely these areas are at night, when the illuminated skyline provides a striking backdrop for the flotilla of sleek yachts and gleaming powerboats. SportRacingHorse racing Pfieffer takes fresh approach to Ice Kool in Melbourne spring audition Craig Kerry September 17, 2026 — 12:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

David Pfieffer believes a refreshed Ice Kool is primed to bounce back at Randwick on Saturday from a flat performance as the Warwick Farm trainer looks to step the speedster up to stakes grade in Melbourne. Ice Kool’s unbeaten run in Sydney came to an end last start when fourth, two and three-quarter lengths off Hawker Hall, in an 1100m benchmark 88 handicap on July 25 at Randwick. Ice Kool and Jay Ford on their way to winning at Randwick on December 27. Getty Images The four-year-old Zoustar gelding faded after racing forward, three wide without cover, a spot he was able to overcome at his previous start over 1000m in 78 grade. Previously, his only defeat in four starts was seventh in the $3 million Sunlight 3YO Plate (1100m) on the Gold Coast in January. Pfieffer gave Ice Kool a six-week freshen up before he returned with a sharp, front-running trial win at home on September 3, and he was confident the talent will fire again. He nominated him for the $1 million group 2 Shorts over 1200m but opted for the easier task in the last, a benchmark 88 handicap over 1100m.

Advertisement

“He raced a fraction flat,” Pfieffer said of the most recent run. “I know he was three deep, but he’d get away with that in the past, although I know you can’t keep doing that as you go up in grade. “I think he appreciates being kept that bit fresh and obviously being up on pace, but just these little things he does wrong are signs of immaturity and a lot of it comes down to him being a boy in a man’s game. “For now, we’ll just take these baby steps while he’s developing his trade. Even just stepping slow from the gates, it’s just little things he’s doing wrong that aren’t helping him. “But I thought his trial was super. He stepped away from the gates nice, put himself on pace, travelled along at a comfortable tempo without overdoing it. He ran good sectionals without asking a lot of him.

Advertisement

“And his coat, I think come Saturday, it will be the best he’s looked his whole career, and like the old saying goes, when they look good, they race well.” Pfieffer has long planned to test Ice Kool, a $3.80 chance on Saturday, on the straight courses in Melbourne over the spring carnival and he was eyeing the group 2 Schillaci Stakes (1100m) on October 10 at Caulfield. “Getting some experience down at Melbourne will do him good and, let’s be honest, he doesn’t need to be taking on these sprinters heading to the Everest, unless he comes out and blows them away on Saturday,” he said. “Then you might rethink and go, do we throw him in the Premiere? But at this stage, you are taking the safer play.” At Newcastle on Friday, Pfieffer has Oh Diamond Lil ($4) from gate one in the group 3 Tibbie Stakes. She was sixth first-up in the Mona Lisa Stakes.

Advertisement

“She was three deep for a bit then she had to push across and get to the front,” he said. “I just don’t think she got that mid-race breather, and being a six-year-old mare now, she’s probably holding a bit more condition and the fitter horses had her covered. “She wasn’t beaten far, her sectionals were still strong. They went five lengths above average mid-race, so that’s going to test a lot of horses out first-up. She’s come out of it well.”

title: Absurd and exciting, this surreal romp will keep you entertained
text:
Advertisement

Key points DANCE: Harrison Ritchie-Jones and Michaela Tancheff perform R.A.I.N at Arts House

MUSIC: Belle and Sebastian return to the Palais with If You’re Feeling Sinister

MUSIC: Cellist Pieter Wispelwey explores solo suites by Benjamin Britten

DANCE: Hobart’s Nelipot Collective bring Our Last Tree to La Mama

OPERA: Lyric Opera put on a Regency-Era Serse at the Gasworks Theatre

DANCE

R.A.I.N ★★★★

Arts House, North Melbourne, until September 20 There’s nothing quite like the shared movement language of Harrison Ritchie-Jones and Michaela Tancheff. Their vocabulary of sporty grappling and mutual manipulation, first seen several years ago in the excellent Cuddle, combines rough-handling with exquisite responsiveness and apparent sensitivity. Harrison Ritchie-Jones and Michaela Tancheff in a scene from R.A.I.N. Darren Gill The opening section of their latest collaboration has playful echoes of a ballroom routine. Extravagant lifts and twists and shifts of momentum also suggest a wrestling contest, with each dancer constantly tracing the other’s body to maintain contact, seeking ways to connect their repertoire of moves. As in Cuddle, they keep up a murmured dialogue, discussing their options and deciding what comes next. Moves are named like invitations which can be accepted or rejected. These casual exchanges make the choreography seem negotiated live: an intricate physical conversation with its own laconic commentary.

Advertisement

Paradoxically, this verbal back and forth makes us more aware of who initiates and who responds, inviting us to diagnose power relations in the mechanics of partnering. Or, at the very least, it draws attention to the contrast in their stage personalities: one expansive and eager, the other more reserved and reactive. Structurally, the development of the show from scene to scene feels a little arbitrary. Of course, the unexpected twists and turns are part of the fun, but I think I would have enjoyed this show even more if there was a clearer sense of narrative progress. The casual exchanges in R.A.I.N make the choreography seem negotiated live. Darren Gill Ritchie-Jones’s program statement describes pushing their partnering practice to its limits and exploring how it fails. But what are the stakes? Does apparent failure count as success for the performers, or is the other way around? It sounds a little too much like navel gazing. Fortunately, the absurdities of this surreal romp are sufficiently entertaining: horse-riding antics, a sudden mystifying leap into opera, crazy costumes and multiple unexpected bursts of song. There’s more than enough excitement at the surface to keep us from looking deeper.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

MUSIC

Belle and Sebastian ★★★★★

Palais Theatre, September 12 “Welcome to the second recording session for this still quite-new band,” Stuart Murdoch says with a grin. His tongue is firmly in cheek – Belle and Sebastian, the indie-pop group he’s led for more than half his life, is on tour celebrating its 30th year. In 1996, the bookish Scots made their debut with two albums: Tigermilk and If You’re Feeling Sinister. On this anniversary tour, they’re alternating playing those records in full. Melbourne gets the Sinister treatment. Belle & Sebastian perform at the Palais, September 12, 2026. Richard Clifford Playing albums in full live can be a cynical cash-cow in the age of commodified nostalgia, but there’s no denying the sheer delight of hearing a beloved album like this in all its glory. On record, Sinister’s arrangements are delicate; live, they’re injected with a shot of joyous energy, with buzzing synth to boot. Many of these songs begin with Murdoch alone, singing with that sweet, instantly recognisable voice, before the eight other musicians on stage slowly blossom to create sunlight in musical form. Lead guitarist Stevie Jackson raucously takes on the harmonica for Me and the Major, his movements a chaotic blur.

Advertisement

As the album reaches its halfway point, a projection behind the band shows the LP being flipped on a turntable – “a bit of antiquated attention to detail,” Murdoch says. Eager fans have been dancing in the aisles from the beginning, but when the band plays Get Me Away, I’m Dying, the entire venue is on its feet. The gorgeous Mayfly is another highlight from this half, but really, it’s all joy, not least because Murdoch and co are clearly having a blast, too. Murdoch’s signature humour is on display all night as he intersperses the music with quips, including a spiel about Victoria’s slogans as seen on number plates and a joke about Viagra as he takes his medication on stage. “Back to sweetness and light!” he says, and back they go. Sarah Martin, Stuart Murdoch and Stevie Jackson of Belle & Sebastian. Richard Clifford A guitar-heavy I’m a Cuckoo kicks off the second set, comprising songs from the rest of the band’s long career. Belle and Sebastian have such a varied discography that it’s a grab-bag every night. There are some deeper cuts here, such as 2010’s Little Lou, Ugly Jack, Prophet John, recorded with Norah Jones; here, it’s long-time vocalist Sarah Martin who does the honours, beautiful as ever. 2006’s Funny Little Frog is a charming, nostalgic treat. The band is pulling songs out on the fly by the end, with Another Sunny Day closing the night. It’s apt – with 30 years of sunny days up their sleeves, Belle and Sebastian keep on delivering.

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

MUSIC

Pieter Wispelwey with Piers Lane ★★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, September 15 Pure genius. These two words arguably encapsulate the astonishing imagination behind the three solo suites that Benjamin Britten composed for the Russian cellist Mstislav Rostropovich between 1964 and 1971. Taking Bach’s fabled cello suites as a model, these tours de force remain revolutionary in pushing the instrument’s boundaries of timbre and texture. Pieter Wispelwey performs at Melbourne Recital Centre, September 15, 2026 Laura Manariti Over three evenings, Dutch cellist Pieter Wispelwey, long an ardent and persuasive exponent of these works, is performing programs centred around each suite. Prokofiev and Shostakovich were appropriate stablemates in the series opener, not least because Prokofiev wrote his Cello Sonata in C, Op. 119 for Rostropovich, but also that the cellist was part of the deep friendship and admiration shared between himself, Shostakovich and Britten.

Advertisement

Providing the first taste of Wispelwey’s chameleonic way with his 1760 Guadagnini cello, the Prokofiev ran the gamut of emotions, starting with its dark, sombre opening before flowering into rich lyricism, moments of childlike wonder and folkloric exuberance. Britten’s Cello Suite No. 1, Op. 72 was full of ear-bending marvels, including a witty, cleverly constructed fugue and an evocative march in which the masterly bouncing of the bow summoned up martial images. A stunning moto perpetuo led to the return of the imposing, unifying Canto. Few others would be capable of bringing this music alive so vibrantly and comprehensibly. Pianist Piers Lane’s committed partnership was entirely empathetic Laura Manariti Wispelwey ensured Shostakovich’s Cello Sonata in D minor, Op. 40 brimmed over with fascinating detail; bringing richly burnished tone to the eerie opening melody and plaintive Largo, unerring technique to the manic second movement and cheeky playfulness to the finale. Here and in the Prokofiev, pianist Piers Lane’s committed partnership was entirely empathetic. Setting aside the substandard printed program that doesn’t even list the movements of the works performed, don’t miss the remaining two opportunities to hear astounding music performed by musicians of genius.

Reviewed by Tony Way

Advertisement

DANCE

Our Last Tree ★★★

La Mama, until September 18 Hobart’s Nelipot Collective bring something we rarely see on Melbourne stages: unpretentiously referential contemporary dance. Their latest show, Our Last Tree, points us with a sort of guileless enthusiasm towards the green earth and its wonders. Nelipot Collective perform Our Last Tree as part of La Mama’s Hope Punk Climate Festival Darren Gill Sometimes the relentless self-reflexivity of our local choreographers – their unwillingness to make work about the world beyond the stage – can seem like a fear of artistic failure. Nelipot embrace that fear with an earnest, wilfully naive fable of loss and recovery. Certainly, their slightly manic smiles and touchy-feely involvement of the audience suggest a community-oriented performance. You can imagine them at a farmers’ market, amid haybales and squealing children munching on small-batch fudge.

Advertisement

And yet I find their evocation of the life of the forest compelling. What they do best here is suggest – with reaching, serpentine limbs – the way that forests envelop us completely, above and below and all around. The intimate stage at La Mama, further compressed by the placement of a cardboard tree along one side, suits these densely convolved bodies. They seem to fill the space completely, coiling themselves into any chink of vacancy. Composer and violist Andrea Breen accompanies the performance with catchy, rather grand melodic hooks, which she returns to between wandering passages. Her music suggests something rooted yet inexorably moving, a tree’s stillness alive with change. Her score also implies a fuller orchestration: I hear the ghosts of horns and oboes underneath it. And yet the exposed solo voice suggests kinship with the last tree. Haunting, effective and beautifully played. Other production elements are less impressive. The slime-green tulle and the cardboard trunk (endearingly ornamented with hand-drawn growth rings) suggest a production for children; I suspect a younger audience would respond well. Yes, the work could be called unsophisticated, but only if that also means a refreshing independence from convention, as well as the courage to approach their subject directly.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

OPERA

Serse ★★

Gasworks Theatre, until September 13 We’re all getting restless. Twenty minutes after the curtain was meant to go up for the opening show of Lyric Opera’s Serse, we’re still waiting for the conductor to raise his baton. Eventually, company artistic director and conductor Patrick Burns addresses the audience, explaining that though they’ve tried to fix the issue, they’ve had no success. Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne Jodie Hutchinson Both projectors have died. For the near-three-hour Italian opera we’re about to witness, there will be no surtitles. No translations. Oh dear. Turns out, if it was sung in English, it’d be hard to follow anyway. Handel’s 1738 opera about the King of Persia is one of those operas stacked with couples pursuing, deceiving, rejecting and reuniting with one another, plus disguises and mistaken identities thrown in, of course.

Advertisement

Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne, but for a company that has commendably programmed contemporary operas in previous seasons, Serse is, frankly, an odd choice. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever, updated to the Regency era where it fits quite well, what with all the letter-writing and love-in-turmoil. But even with tech issues aside, faults remain. The ornamentation demands were too much for some, and the approach (though it is correct Baroque style) of leaving out vibrato resulted in some unenergised vocal patches. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever. Jodie Hutchinson Some shined, like mezzo Naomi Flatman, who with a honeyed, resonant sound, delivered the standout performance of the night. Soprano Rebecca Rashleigh too gave a consistently vibrant performance, with thrilling top notes. As Serse, it was testament to Sally-Anne Russell’s comedic talent that though we mostly had no idea what was going on, people still laughed when they were, presumably, meant to. Though it was the initial problem, the ensuing convoluted plot, repetitive musical style and uneven singing proved that being sung in a foreign language is not the greatest measure of an opera’s accessibility.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

DANCE

7 Dances for 7 People ★★★

Northcote Town Hall, until September 19 Yes, there are indeed seven dances – or sections – in choreographer Trá Mi Dinh’s latest work, but only the first of them is unambiguously successful. I would happily have watched this strange, lustrous gambit for the full hour, either extended or simply repeated. Tra Mi Dinh and Rachel Coulson in 7 Dances for 7 People. Darren Gill Two dancers emerge from billowing clouds of smoke, like figures in a dream, amid an eerie tintinnabulation. Delicate unison stepping gives their progress toward the audience an insect-like grace; raised arms and joined hands further heighten their otherworldly appearance. The awkward position of the arms, which restricts the movement of the upper body, creates a sense of fragility and risk. It’s as if their grip on one another is all that prevents them tumbling back in the cloud of smoke. It gives the whole scene a shimmery, slippery sort of ephemerality.

Advertisement

After the first dance, the movement becomes more eclectic. Smooth isolations, with their tensing and releasing, give way to looser spinning figures. Vaguely balletic poses contrast with thrusting modern dance gestures. And everything whirls together in the smoke. The combinations are not always compelling, but something of the mysterious atmosphere of the first section persists. And interesting details register throughout, particularly in the way the seven dancers move between pairs and trios, with new arrangement materialising in the gloom. The balletic poses contrast with modern dance gestures as everything whirls together amid the smoke. Darren Gill This show is based on a shorter commission for Lucy Guerin’s Pieces in 2024, and it retains the same production team, including lighting designer Rachel Rui Qian Lee and costume designer Geoffrey Watson, who provides beautiful filmy smocks. Tilman Robinson’s score feels a little too insistent. The opening section with its bells has an attractive alienness, but I think the heavier beats used thereafter impose too much on the choreography and a more ambient soundscape might have been more effective.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Updated

Arts Second strike planned by Arts Centre Melbourne employees The work is apparently based on the significance of the number seven across religions and cultural traditions. Yet it is strongest when there is no theme: just fleeting relations between bodies – repetitions and doublings, divergences and singularities – in a world before number settles into meaning.

title: ‘Go to hell’: Students storm CBD over Hanson

Hundreds of students have taken to the streets of Sydney to protest against Pauline Hanson and the rise of One Nation.

The gathering kicked off in Hyde Park in the CBD on Thursday afternoon.

The protesters began chanting "Pauline Hanson go to hell, take your racists there as well," before storming down Market St

The mood quickly turned rowdy as organisers chanted "when I say Pauline, you say f*ck off".

Thursday's rallies follows similar protests in August.

title: How Australia's migration system is about to change
text:
WHAT'S HAPPENING WITH MIGRATION?

* International students and those on graduate visas will no longer be allowed to bring family members with them to Australia, with some exceptions including for PhD students

* Only 45,000 working holiday-makers will be able to stay in Australia for a second year, and only 5000 for a third year - down from 57,000 and 31,000 respectively, but a slow-down to the processing of those visas will end for everyone except British citizens

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

* Migrants coming to work in construction, farming, fisheries, mining and teaching will be prioritised

* Only foreign students transferring to higher-level courses (bachelor's to master's for example) will be able to extend their visas

* People who overstay their visa, of which there are about 77,000, will be sent to detention centres, with the government now on the hunt for more facilities, compliance officers and beds

* The points test, which determines which skilled migrants come to Australia, will be revamped to consider construction-related qualifications as equivalent to university degrees

* Powers to punish and de-register dodgy migration agents, who help foreigners get Australian visas, will expand

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

WHY THE CHANGES?

* The government is trying to bring Australia's population growth due to migration down from 292,100 to 245,000 in the year to July 2027 and 225,000 each year thereafter, and to curb visa-hopping, "rorting" and "gaming" the system

* That figure has stubbornly exceeded Labor's forecasts since the party came to power in 2022, but Immigration Minister Tony Burke said migration was now tracking in line with its targets

* The coalition believes the figure should descend to 170,000 in line with housing construction, and One Nation wants a 130,000-person a year cap

HOW ARE THEY BEING IMPLEMENTED?

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

* The changes may not be law because negotiations between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor broke down in the week before Mr Burke's address, dooming hope of getting reforms through the Senate

* Without parliament's approval, the government cannot proceed with a desired crackdown on phoney asylum-seekers' claims

* But Mr Burke insisted negotiations with the coalition were ongoing and productive, and said "we have put nothing forward that is a wedge to them".
